papers.title: Putting a Robot on a Phone Call: Layered Signaling, Bounded Occupancy and Turn Arbitration over WebRTC
papers.authors: Zheyuan Zhang, Zaide Zhang
papers.abstract: We put a Thor robot on a browser voice call, with speech sent from Safari, answers played through the robot's loudspeaker and transcripts returned to the phone. We separate HTTPS signaling, relayed WebRTC media and speech generation into independently observable routes. The browser prefetches relay credentials and allows a 500 ms window after its first relay candidate. The backend starts speech and WebRTC-answer preparation concurrently within a 55 s deadline. A session slot and a non-blocking speaker lock coordinate calls with local voice access. A 2 s gate gives the controller an opportunity to suppress chat before playback. Fifteen of sixteen first dials reached ready-to-speak, comprising seven of eight Wi-Fi calls with a median of 5.57 s and eight of eight cellular calls with a median of 6.76 s. All twenty scored occupancy and recovery scenarios admitted a later call. During five 60 s outages, the backend released the line while the phone remained offline. Across 40 controlled replays, enabling the gate suppressed chat when the controller decided at 1 s. At 3 s, chat and controller feedback both played in sequence, with no overlapping output in any trace. Two additional boundary traces exposed a receipt naming a later feedback item and a new call's query returning its predecessor's feedback. These measurements cover application events on one platform and simulated controller decisions, with acoustic output and task correctness outside their scope.

papers.title: PreWAM: Exploring the Design of Latent Future Prediction for World-Action Modeling
papers.authors: Wan Chi, Sen Li, Zihang Cui, Chuqin Huang, Yunlong Wang, Nanshan Deng, Yanjun Huang
papers.abstract: World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts.

papers.title: PoseVLN: Learning Geometric State Evolution for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.authors: Pengyu Hou, Mingfei Han, Haihong Hao, Xiaolong Wu, Bo Dong, Xiaojun Chang, Salman Khan, Bin Shi
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to relate past experience, current spatial state, and future motion while following natural-language instructions. Recent approaches improve these capabilities through long-horizon memory, state-aware reasoning, and future prediction, yet these components are often modeled separately, leaving navigation state evolution insufficiently connected across time. We argue that camera pose provides a natural geometric representation for bridging past, present, and future states. Based on this insight, we propose PoseVLN, a pose-aware VLN framework that jointly learns navigation decisions and geometric state evolution. PoseVLN organizes visual memory and the current observation in an episode-relative coordinate frame, and jointly predicts the next K navigation actions together with a local $Δ$Pose over the same horizon. The predicted $Δ$Pose is composed with the current trajectory-level pose to obtain the future pose state, which is recursively propagated throughout navigation, forming a continuous geometric state evolution from past memory to future motion. Experiments on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen splits demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling geometric state evolution, with PoseVLN outperforming the strongest compared baselines by 2.6 and 2.9 percentage points in success rate, respectively, using only single RGB observations.

papers.title: Physicl Scenes: An Artist-created 3D Dataset for Learning Perception and Action
papers.authors: Yueh-Cheng Liu, Snehal Jauhri, Matthias Nießner, Angela Dai
papers.abstract: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.

papers.title: Perception Is Enough, at the Right Scale: Scale-Adaptive Token Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Yifeng Lin, Liuxiang Qiu, Yunfeng Chen, Tiesong Zhao
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $τ$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $τ$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.

papers.title: POISE: Curvature-Aware Critic Regularization for Smooth Actor-Critic Control
papers.authors: Jeong Woon Lee, Namho Kim, Hyoseok Hwang
papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods achieve high returns in robotic control, yet trained actors exhibit high-frequency action oscillations. Most smoothness methods constrain the actor, whereas PAVE regularizes the critic by separately penalizing action-gradient variation and encouraging negative action curvature. The same gradient change, however, moves the critic's preferred action farther where the critic is flat, and separate penalties do not measure this motion. We characterize this motion through the greedy shift, which approximates greedy-action displacement across state transitions to first order under local concavity. Since displacement alone does not reflect its critic-value consequences, the analysis further shows that the shift's curvature-weighted energy approximates the value lost by retaining the previous greedy action to second order. Based on this relationship, POISE regularizes the curvature-weighted energy along temporal and spatial state displacements. It employs a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling while leaving the actor unchanged. On six continuous control tasks with TD3, POISE reduces the smoothness score on every task by $5.9\times$ on average ($4.5\times$ geometric mean), compared with $2.2\times$ ($1.9\times$) for the strongest baseline, and achieves the lowest score on five tasks. Paired return intervals include zero on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.

papers.title: OnCue: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios under Occlusion with Temporal Control
papers.authors: Kailang Ma, Li Song, Weining Ren, Zirui Li, Xianjie Dai, Jingguang Li, Zuyi Guo, Benwang Chen, et al.
papers.abstract: Occluded hazards challenge autonomous driving because visibility timing determines available avoidance actions. Existing scenario generators control hazard motion without jointly specifying exposure and reference-contact times. We propose OnCue, a framework that generates safety-critical encounters in real driving logs with these temporal conditions. Scene geometry provides hidden starts and timed waypoints for pedestrian, cyclist, and vehicle trajectory generation. An offline response oracle labels encounters as Reactive (avoidable after exposure) or Anticipatory (avoidable only with earlier visibility) and stores safe maneuvers as training demonstrations. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, 90.1-96.6% of valid trajectories meet both requested times within +/-0.2 s. OnCue matches the requested reaction window between them in 92.8% of shared vehicle requests versus at most 42.1% for adapted adversarial generators. Across matched cyclist encounters, longer windows lower PDM-Closed collision from 59.1% to 5.5%, while the learned planner LatentDriver shows the opposite trend. OnCue demonstrations reduce LatentDriver target collision by 54.8 points on held-out Reactive tests, but reduce overall no-target progress by 12.7 m. These results highlight the value of temporal control for evaluating and improving planners under occlusion.

papers.title: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
papers.authors: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu, Shengfeng He
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

papers.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
papers.authors: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Jiayuan Yan, Bohan Fang, Wisdom Oluchi Ikezogwo, Ainaz Eftekhar, Max Argus, Jason Ren, et al.
papers.abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/

papers.title: ObsBridge: Observation-Grounded Conditioning for Ego Trajectory Prediction
papers.authors: Zhenhao Wang, Shaofeng Liang, Jiemin Wu, Sijia Chen, Keni Shi, Nan Li, Wenshuo Chen, Bowen Tian, et al.
papers.abstract: Pedestrian forecasting from ego-view observations is challenging because occlusion, limited visibility, and tracking errors corrupt observed motion histories. Such errors are particularly consequential for autonomous robot navigation. Existing paradigms typically either impute noisy history positions before forecasting or jointly train an auxiliary history reconstruction branch. However, predictors trained on clean histories may be sensitive to residual errors in recovered histories at deployment. Meanwhile, auxiliary reconstruction still computes inter-agent interactions over raw, corrupted coordinates. We investigate conditioning future prediction on both recovered historical states and raw observation evidence, with progressive training to accommodate imperfect recovery. Building on this insight, we propose ObsBridge, a flow-based trajectory forecasting framework with observation-grounded historical bridging. Specifically, ObsBridge first employs a frozen estimator to recover historical motion from agent-relative and ego-relative positions, image-plane locations, and visibility states. During training, we introduce an agent-wise curriculum that gradually replaces clean teacher histories with complete estimated histories before context encoding. This progressively exposes the predictor to estimated histories during training. Furthermore, we design a residual geometry adapter to fuse the encoded motion with original observation evidence. We aggregate the resulting representations through social attention to condition the flow-based trajectory generator. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that ObsBridge outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On EgoTraj-TBD, it reduces minADE@20 by 6.5\% and minFDE@20 by 8.7\%. The code will be provided at https://github.com/shawnliang420/ObsBridge.

papers.title: OVOK: A Recursive Self-Improving Agentic Framework for Video-Based Articulated Robot State Estimation
papers.authors: Cheng Dai, Renkai Luo, Guanfeng Tang, Siming Li, Hao Zhao
papers.abstract: Recovering articulated robot state from video supports metric spatial sensing for manipulation, scene reconstruction, and action planning. Yet the problem is ill-posed: different intrinsics, camera-to-robot poses, and joint angles can explain similar observations. Prior task-specific regressors typically assume known intrinsics, fit one robot through laborious data collection and robot-specific training, and still transfer poorly across scenes. Foundation models apply to any robot zero-shot, but their estimates have large errors. We present OVOK (One Video to Kinetics), a recursive self-improving agentic framework for this task. Under a human-authored protocol, an agentic initializer constructs robot-specific OVOK-4k; a proposer--executor--verifier loop then jointly evolves tools and executable workflows from feedback. Updated tools and workflows are accepted only when the verifier judges a positive improvement. The retained workflow is frozen for accurate inference. Experiments demonstrate that the evolved workflow achieves state-of-the-art results on DREAM-V and RoboKeyGen-V, delivering robust and accurate estimates.

papers.title: Next-Manip: On-Demand Agent-Policy Collaboration for Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Jiayi Liu, Ke Ye, Jiaming Zhou, Yufei Huang, Haotian Liang, Kun-Yu Lin, Junwei Liang
papers.abstract: General-purpose robotic manipulation requires task reasoning, failure recovery, and precise control, yet limited manipulation data make these abilities difficult to obtain from a single policy. Recent multimodal agents show promise in task reasoning and recovery but lack reliable fine-grained control and incur high inference cost, whereas learned policies provide efficient fine-grained execution but struggle beyond their learned skills. Although their complementary strengths suggest combining the two, doing so requires repeatedly deciding which executor should act as task demands change. Instead of relying on the agent for each decision, we present Next-Manip, an on-demand agent--policy collaboration framework that decouples executor allocation from costly agent inference. We propose an Agent Invocation Controller (AIC) that allocates control between the policy and the agent through a lightweight classifier of current execution demands. We further introduce Task Dynamics Context (TDC), which packages informative manipulation changes from in-context examples into compact task references to support both agent reasoning and executor allocation. Across two simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments, Next-Manip achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing agent inference costs.

papers.title: NativeDrive: Native Multimodal Foundations for Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Zehua Fan, Qi Jiang, Wei Li, Kai Tang, Yue Jiang, Yujian Li, Bailin Li, Feng Gao, et al.
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires semantic understanding and fine-grained scene perception for precise action prediction. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit semantic priors, but low-dimensional action labels provide limited structural supervision. Some studies extend VLAs with visual generation tasks or adopt video-based world-action models (WAMs), but both approaches introduce appearance-reconstruction overhead, which is less relevant to planning. Native multimodal models offer an alternative to unify understanding and generation within one backbone. On this basis, we propose NativeDrive, a native encoder-free multimodal driving framework adapting the unified backbone for policy learning and introduce a dense supervision task tailored to driving. The Native Action Interface reuses the understanding expert's token-prediction interface for the discrete policy and adapts the generation expert for continuous policy. Driving Semantic Editing reuses the generation expert's editing capability for dense scene-structure supervision during training, while inference runs only the selected planning policy. NativeDrive achieves competitive planning performance among unified understanding-and-generation models on NAVSIM v1 and v2, with ablations validating its components' effectiveness. papers.title: Motion Conditioned World Modeling for Embodied Visual Tracking
papers.authors: Jiahao Zhang, Xuan Yao, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
papers.abstract: World models support embodied decision-making by predicting future environment states. In embodied visual tracking, uncertain target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes jointly affect visual observations, making future-state prediction challenging. We propose Motion-Conditioned World Modeling, which incorporates predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion into latent state transitions. A Geometry--Progress module jointly models geometric paths and single-step travel distances through shared motion modes and path-conditioned progress distributions. This formulation captures uncertainty in route selection and motion progress while preserving their dependence. Action-induced coordinate transformations express predicted paths in the next robot frame, providing geometrically grounded conditions for future visual-state prediction. Future visual feature reconstruction supervises the motion predictor through the conditioned transition branch, linking explicit motion representations to subsequent observations. The model is jointly optimized with motion likelihood, feature reconstruction, and expert-action supervision, enabling the tracking policy to combine visual context with predictive motion cues.Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks demonstrate improved tracking performance and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight $0.5$B backbone.

papers.title: Motion Chain of Thought: Disentangling Motion Semantics from Visual Appearance for Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Xiangkai Ma, Xinyi Wang, Junjie Wang, Sheng Xu, Mingyang Li, Yue Ma, Han Zhang, Yuzheng Zhuang, et al.
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) aim to construct a unified architecture capable of understanding world state evolution and guiding action generation. However, existing visual branches focus on predicting static visual observation, rather than reflecting potential transition information that captures the evolution of world states under motion interactions. This leads to representational entanglement between high-level physical condition evolution and low-level action trajectory generation within the Action Model, creating a structural bottleneck while weakening the predictive capability of world evolution modeling for action generation. We propose PILOT (Physical Inference for Latent Optimized Trajectories), whose core Representational Deduction (RD) bridges this gap by integrating motion chain-of-thought (CoT) guidance as a native model capability. Specifically, RD aims to encourage the action branch to explicitly model potential state transition tokens, which are retained as CoT in the reasoning space to guide fine-grained motion trajectory. Experiments demonstrate that RD not only improves the success rate and generalization ability of WAMs in complex robotic manipulation tasks but also enhances the model's physical interpretability by decoupling high-level motion semantics from low-level trajectory details. Furthermore, the abundant state transition supervision signals introduced by RD effectively alleviate the sparse supervision in action generation, supporting data-efficient real-robot adaptation with reduced demonstration sets.

papers.title: MemHand: Memory-Enhanced World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
papers.authors: Junyi Ma, Zhangshuo Qi, Erhang Zhang, Mingjie Li, Hesheng Wang
papers.abstract: Recovering the continuous world-space motion of both hands from egocentric video is essential for applications such as human-to-robot policy transfer and augmented reality. Achieving this goes beyond reconstructing the hands from each individual frame, as the context that a frame needs is often spread over time, especially around occlusions or when a hand moves out of sight. Recent works have explored how to exploit temporal context, yet they mostly draw it from fixed-length windows. Such windows cannot guarantee that every frame has the context required to reconstruct the hands in world space with accurate poses and metric scale. To address this limitation, we introduce MemHand, a memory-enhanced framework for world-space hand motion reconstruction. MemHand maintains two complementary forms of memory. The Short-Term Event Memory keeps the context of the well-observed hand around each occlusion or out-of-sight event and supplies it to frames with weak or missing visual evidence. In addition, since the metric scale holds over the whole recording, the Long-Term Scale Memory retains the most reliable observations across the video as scale anchors within a bounded state. Across benchmarks featuring severe occlusions and frequent out-of-sight intervals, MemHand achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and generalizes well to unseen domains. Benefiting from the synergy of both memories, it cuts W-MPJPE by 57\% on ARCTIC and 70\% on HOT3D relative to StableHand, delivering continuous and metrically accurate world-space hand poses and trajectories. papers.title: Many Senses, One World: Learning Hierarchical Multimodal World Representations for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Jin Yang, Youlin Wang, Ping Wei
papers.abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation relies on multimodal inputs that capture visual context and non-visual physical interaction cues for precise and coordinated control. To address the challenge of effectively integrating these modalities for policy learning, we propose HiMoDex, a two-stage framework centered on hierarchical multimodal world-state representations. In Stage 1, we pretrain a hierarchical representation network on the collected dataset of 1.19 million synchronized multimodal time steps. The network integrates visual context with tactile, force-torque, and audio cues into unified world-state embeddings. In Stage 2, we freeze the pretrained network and use its embeddings to condition a shared world-action transformer. The transformer jointly learns action generation and action-conditioned future-state prediction. Experiments across five real-world tasks show that HiMoDex achieves an average success rate of 78.7\%, representing an absolute improvement of 32.0\% over the strongest evaluated baseline. Extensive ablations validate the benefits of hierarchical representation learning and two-stage training. Failure analysis helps explain performance differences across variants. papers.title: MXI-MemICL: Towards In-Context Robot Manipulation through Self-Retrieved Interaction Memory
papers.authors: Jialong Peng, Shihao Zhou, Feng Yan, Wen Xiao, Haozheng Wang, Wenqi Ren, Wenyuan Sheng, Jian Qiao, et al.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates. However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision-language-action (VLA) models. By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations. Specifically, a visual-action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution. To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent and uses it to query memory. The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence. MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0. Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks. The code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: MRCT: An Object-Centric Two-Layer Control Architecture for Heavy-Payload Multi-Robot Transportation
papers.authors: Ning Wang, Yoshihiko Nakamura, Tianwei Zhang
papers.abstract: Cooperative transportation of heavy payloads by heterogeneous mobile manipulators requires coordinated payload motion, force distribution, and compliant physical interaction. This paper presents MRCT, an object-centric two-layer control architecture for multi-robot transportation. At the object level, a model predictive controller (MPC) generates a coordinated contact-force reference for the payload. At the robot level, whole- body impedance control (WBIC) modules on individual robots realise the reference through a confidence-based blending of velocity-tracking and impedance torques. The blending mechanism emphasises tracking when the joint-velocity error is small and increases compliance when tracking degrades because of abrupt reference changes or physical disturbances. Simulation and hardware experiments with a heterogeneous team comprising a single-arm and a dual-arm mobile manipulator transporting a near-rated table payload demonstrate accurate object tracking, regulated contact forces, and stable payload orientation. Parameter sensitivity studies, obstacle-avoidance transportation, and step-load disturbance experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of MRCT for reliable cooperative transportation under the evaluated conditions

papers.title: MRBench: Benchmarking Physical Necessity Reasoning in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Yanzhe Chen, Zhijun Cao, Ruihe An, Chang Gong, Mike Zheng Shou
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-robot manipulation have shown how robots can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. However, successful coordination does not reveal which robots are actually needed. The same task may require different teams as robot capabilities change, resources become unavailable, or objects replace robotic support. We argue that reliable multi-robot manipulation requires physical necessity reasoning: understanding what a task demands, which resources can fulfill those demands, and which are truly necessary. We introduce MRBench, a benchmark for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation. It comprises eight tasks with distinct concurrency and reach constraints, each evaluated under five configurations that change the required resources while preserving the task goal. Our evaluation reveals that existing coordination agents perform well with reference teams but struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support. To address this gap, we propose MRScissors, which separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities and identifies minimal feasible teams through constrained search. Across two model backbones, MRScissors achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points, respectively. Together, these findings expose a critical gap between coordinating robots and understanding their physical necessity.

papers.title: MARGIN: A Risk-Aware Agent for Robot Program Refinement
papers.authors: Hongbo Duan, Fan Du, Haipeng Luo, Bin Qian, Zichao Nie, Yilin Mi, Yaopeng Tian, Jiake Tian, et al.
papers.abstract: Robot-programming agents improve executable control policies through repeated testing and repair, yet binary success saturates while execution risk persists across unseen scenes. We introduce MARGIN, a risk-aware agent that converts successful robot rollouts into actionable evidence for program refinement. Its near-miss margin measures the fraction of the execution budget remaining in the slowest successful development rollout. The agent uses this signal to prioritize fragile programs, guide targeted repairs, and select revisions that preserve development success while increasing execution headroom. An exact safe-racing rule accelerates success-based candidate evaluation. We evaluate MARGIN across LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-90, and Robosuite. In our 80-task LIBERO-Pro reproduction, 78 programs attain perfect development success while accounting for substantial failures on unseen seeds. The near-miss margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774, and low-margin programs exhibit 2.97 times higher failure risk. Across two independent evaluation rounds spanning 37 unique LIBERO-Pro tasks, MARGIN reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0%, with reductions of 18.0-20.0% on LIBERO-90 and Robosuite. Safe racing reduces fixed-sequence candidate-evaluation episodes by 53.5% while retaining identical selections, and paired execution probes improve acceptance decisions by identifying hidden regressions. Together, these results establish near-miss evidence as an effective basis for risk-aware, budget-efficient robot program refinement.

papers.title: Lost on Campus: Evaluating Embodied Spatial Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in the Wild
papers.authors: Zehan Zheng, Yanyuan Chen, Deming Li, Yutao Tang, Jianwen Xie, Alan Yuille, Jieneng Chen, Cheng Peng
papers.abstract: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.

papers.title: LookAnything: A Foundation Model for Holistic Gaze Following
papers.authors: Jiayu Tang, Yuchen Zhou, Hongsheng Wu, Hanjing Ye, Ke Huang, Cheng Wang, Yuqin Dai, Yufei Huang, et al.
papers.abstract: Human gaze provides a rich window into attention and intent, making its understanding essential for applications ranging from social signal analysis to human-robot interaction. Existing methods typically employ highly customized architectures relying on auxiliary inputs like head crops or depth maps, causing cascading errors and inference overhead. Trained on single domains and confined to isolated gaze following with heatmap outputs, they lack flexibility and generalization for diverse interactive scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present LookAnything, a foundation model that unifies diverse gaze-centric tasks for holistic gaze following. Benefiting from large-scale multi-task and cross-domain training, LookAnything flexibly adapts to various settings, generating diverse outputs (points, boxes, heatmaps, and language) and supporting broad gaze-centric localization, description, and reasoning. At its core, we introduce learnable gaze-prior queries to promote gaze-aware representation learning, eliminating the need for auxiliary external inputs. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct HoliGaze, a comprehensive corpus and benchmark comprising 311K question-answer pairs across 5 capability dimensions and 9 distinct tasks. Experiments demonstrate that LookAnything consistently outperforms 33 leading vision-language models on holistic gaze following, while remaining highly competitive with dedicated specialists across 5 conventional target detection benchmarks. Evaluation on unseen datasets and deployment on a real robot further validate its strong out-of-domain generalization and flexible adaptation in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Lecciones aprendidas de la arquitectura cognitiva para robots CORTEX
papers.authors: Pablo Bustos, Alejandro Torrejón, Jorge Alonso Uribe Calderón, Shahriar Hassan
papers.abstract: Este trabajo examina qué ocurre cuando conceptos centrales de la psicología Cognitiva —memoria de trabajo, procesos atencionales, imaginación prospectiva y formación de categorías— se interpretan en un sistema robótico autónomo que debe funcionar en tiempo real en entornos humanos. El vehículo de este examen es CORTEX (Cognitive Robotics Architecture), una arquitectura cognitiva para robots desarrollada durante más de una década, cuyo diseño ha estado inspirado parcialmente por teorías psicológicas y neurocientíficas. El artículo describe las decisiones de diseño que han configurado CORTEX, los compromisos que han exigido y las tensiones que han revelado entre la formulación funcional de los modelos teóricos y las restricciones de un agente físico que actúa bajo incertidumbre y recursos limitados. Este estudio sugiere que la robótica podría actuar como un laboratorio de pruebas para la psicología: la necesidad de programar funciones como la atención o la memoria de trabajo fuerza la transición de constructos teóricos a mecanismos explícitos. Esto permite examinar cuestiones como la organización jerárquica de la representación y la interacción entre sistemas de memoria especializados, la naturaleza de la selectividad atencional bajo restricciones de recursos, o las condiciones que permiten que algo pueda llamarse concepto y no mero patrón estadístico. A partir de este análisis se plantean líneas de trabajo futuro con implicaciones tanto para la robótica cognitiva como para la comprensión teórica de los procesos mentales que la inspiran.

papers.title: Learning When a Robot Should Ask For Help: Adaptive Intervention Requests in Human-Robot Teaming
papers.authors: Yanran Jiang, Cécile Paris, Dana Kulić, Leimin Tian
papers.abstract: Robots operating in complex environments occasionally encounter situations where autonomous navigation fails. Requesting and receiving a timely intervention from their human supervisor can be critical for failure prevention or recovery. However, requesting help too frequently or at inappropriate times can increase operator workload and reduce team efficiency, while delayed requests may lead to prolonged downtime or unrecoverable failures. In addition to alert timing, the human, robot and task context also influences the intervention outcomes. This paper proposes an algorithm for learning to generate adaptive human intervention requests during human-robot teaming. A help-seeking policy is trained via offline reinforcement learning based on past intervention helpfulness and autonomous progress. This learned alert policy enables a robot to selectively request human help when the intervention outcome is likely to be beneficial. We evaluate the proposed policy in different task environments and user expertise levels in simulation, followed by evaluation in a physical user study. Our findings demonstrate that the learned policy improves exploration efficiency, reduces unnecessary alerts, and enhances novice user support without compromising expert performance in real-time human-robot teaming missions.

papers.title: Learning Agent States for Latent Action Modeling
papers.authors: Shaoan Xie, Fan Feng, Peiyuan Zhu, Peter Spirtes, Kun Zhang
papers.abstract: Latent action models (LAMs) learn action-like latents from unlabeled video by coupling frame-pair inference with latent-conditioned prediction, enabling policy and world-model pretraining. However, what the latent must explain depends on the representation space used for action inference and transition prediction. When this space entangles the agent's evolving physical state with visual context, such as background and persistent agent appearance, inferred latents can encode information unrelated to the agent's actions. To address this challenge, we propose Agent-State LAM, which jointly learns a compact agent-state representation and latent actions modeling its transitions. The compact state aggregates dense visual features into a shared space for both action inference and forward prediction. To guide what this state retains, we introduce spatially matched temporal discrimination (SMTD), which trains the state to distinguish its source frame from nearby frames through spatially flexible matching with frozen local visual features. Rather than comparing global frame representations, SMTD scores each frame by emphasizing its strongest local feature matches across spatial locations. This scoring allows background and persistent agent appearance to remain matched across frames despite displacement, making these shared cues less informative for identifying the source frame and encouraging the representation to capture the agent's evolving physical state. Extensive experiments on distracting control tasks and six real robot video datasets demonstrate improved action recovery, downstream control, and world-model prediction. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mid-Push/Agent-State-LAM.

papers.title: LeanWAM: Learning Latent World Action Models from Frozen Video Models
papers.authors: Shaolong Li, Hongze Fu, Joyce Chai, Yinpei Dai
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. However, it remains unclear which future representations a policy actually needs and how compactly they can be represented. Our probing study shows that complementary future representations can be compressed into a few tokens while retaining most of their action-decoding performance. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. With 1.4B parameters and no large-scale embodied pretraining, LeanWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, 12.3--41.5$\times$ faster than representative WAMs. These results demonstrate that compact predictive supervision can transfer video priors to robust and efficient control.

papers.title: Knocked Off Course: Tracing Uncommanded Motion from Perception to Action in Embodied VLAs
papers.authors: Dan Zlotnikov, Nadav Alali, Ohad Ben-Shahar
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable simultaneous processing of egocentric video and textual target descriptions to produce action commands for embodied tracking platforms. However, these platforms rarely move exactly as commanded, in part due to unexpected environmental disturbances such as wind, unleveled terrain, and road bumps. Here we study how such models handle uncommanded egomotion. First, we explore performance across diverse disturbances by benchmarking three tracking VLAs on three datasets. We find that models differ in which environmental disturbances hurt them most, but all are sensitive to sudden target loss. Tracing egomotion from pixels to emitted actions, we identify two gaps. In representation, motion is reliably recovered through explicit relations between frames, but aggressive compression of past frames weakens small-motion readouts. In action, large rotations do reach the decision state, yet the decoded direction carries only a few percent of a mirrored rotation's effect on the turn. Targeting both gaps, we fine-tune one model, Uni-NaVid, on data amounting to just 1.7% of its original training set in a ladder of analysis-motivated variants. These gain 5-22 points after target-loss without degrading clean success; after a smooth loss, the best one improves success by 72% (relative), recovering 76% of its gap to clean. We also show that targeted fine-tuning improves recovery partly via a text-mediated action dependency, without new architecture, large-scale data collection or training from scratch.

papers.title: Keypose or Dense? A Controlled Comparison of Action Representations for Stage-Structured Manipulation
papers.authors: Haizhou Ge, Mengshuo Wang, Zhixing Chen, Lei Han, Chen Wang, Lu Shi, Guyue Zhou, Ruqi Huang
papers.abstract: Most imitation policies that predict chunks of future actions use the dense action representation, in which the chunk holds one control target per step. In stage-structured manipulation, where a task can be divided into stages with definable endpoints, the keypose action representation instead sets each step of the chunk to the endpoint of the stage that step belongs to, and a speed-capped servo supplies the motion. We compare the two in several simulated manipulation tasks and on a real robot, with the same chunk length and matched demonstrations, observations, policy architectures and update budgets; in simulation, each one's execution rule is selected on tuning scenes. When the simulated demonstrations are slowed, paused and rerouted, dense success falls sharply while keypose stays roughly level, across three policy architectures and with endpoints extracted from the recorded demonstrations; keypose also leads under object-size and position shift. With clean demonstrations, keypose leads only when they are scarce and is otherwise close to or behind dense across the simulated tasks, provided that the demonstrations and execution rule suit its executor; when they do not, it falls far below dense. The same dependence on the executor appeared on a real robot learning to open a drawer from human demonstrations: dense succeeded more often, and keypose improved substantially only after its executor's rotation and forward speed were adjusted to the demonstrations. These results suggest that keypose trades sensitivity to such variation in the demonstrations for sensitivity to execution that departs from them.

papers.title: KeyMemVLA: Subtask-Guided Key Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Yongwei Zhang, Tao Chen, Sicheng Ma, Yuanzhe Xing, Pengwei Zhang, Yongen Zhao, Yaoqing Hu, Zhikun She, et al.
papers.abstract: Memory-dependent long-horizon manipulation requires vision-language-action (VLA) policies to infer task progress and recall evidence absent from current observations. Under a limited memory budget, the challenge is to retain history that resolves stage ambiguity and supports subsequent decisions. We present KeyMemVLA, a subtask-guided key memory framework based on progress indication and decision-evidence retention. A two-level annotation process selects subtasks satisfying either criterion and labels their final frames as keyframes to supervise online memory writes. A shared vision-language backbone jointly learns subtask, action, and keyframe prediction. At inference, the policy first predicts the current subtask from the instruction, visual context, and memory, then uses this semantic condition to predict actions and future memory-write positions. Actual observations are retained at the selected times during execution. We introduce KMBench to evaluate active memory retention for decisions across subtasks. Evaluations on RMBench-$M(n)$, RoboTwin-MeM, KMBench, and real-world manipulation tasks show higher average success rates than the compared baselines. Ablation studies and representation analysis support the roles of key memory and explicit task-progress semantics. These results highlight the value of coupling sparse key memory with online progress inference for history-dependent control.

papers.title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds
papers.authors: Qingle Liu, Jieming Li, Pei-lin Li, Shenghan Zheng, Ruize Yang, Sunqi Fan, Deyao Hong, Huan-ang Gao, et al.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.

papers.title: HARI4D: Hand-Articulation Aware 4D Reconstruction of Human-Object Interaction
papers.authors: Semin Kim, Xianghui Xie, Chuqiao Li, Jongyoo Kim, Gerard Pons-Moll
papers.abstract: Reasoning about human-object interaction from RGB cameras is important for gaming, VR environments, and robot learning. We introduce a history-aware object tracker that provides robust and stable tracking. Based on these tracks, we improve the interaction configuration through coarse-to-fine reasoning that follows the order of object manipulation: ReachNet first brings the full body and arms to the object during contact, and TouchNet then finalizes hand articulation according to temporal context and local object geometry. On ARCTIC, unseen in training, our method reduces the object error by 56% and improves hand contact F1 from 0.866 to 0.921 over prior art. Our method recovers accurate full body-object interaction with coherent hand articulations and applies to online videos. Our code and pretrained models will be released.

papers.title: Governing the next generation: a framework for the safe and equitable deployment of artificial intelligence, robotics, and immersive technologies in ophthalmology
papers.authors: Shameer Mohamed Naleer, Safras Mohamed Naleer
papers.abstract: Objective A new generation of technologies – artificial intelligence (AI), AI-guided surgical robotics, and immersive systems including virtual and augmented reality – are transforming ophthalmic practice across diagnoses, surgery, training, and patient engagement. Each domain has generated compelling clinical evidence; each has also exposed governance gaps – that, if unaddressed, risk entrenching inequalities, undermining patient safety, and erode clinical trust. This Mini Review synthesises the governance landscape across all three technology domains. Methods A narrative review of primary evidence, regulatory frameworks, and governance literature was conducted across AI diagnostics, AI-guided robotic surgery, and immersive technology platforms in ophthalmology, with a focus on publications between 2018 to 2026. Results Five cross-cutting governance failures common to all three domains are identified: dataset underrepresentation in training and validation; the absence of equity surveillance in post-deployment monitoring; an interpretability gap at the point of clinical use; an absent regulatory framework for agentic and continuously learning systems; and a lack of structured AI literacy in clinical training. Conclusion We propose a unified five-domain governance framework applicable across AI, robotics, and immersive technology in ophthalmology. Governance should not be a constraint on innovation – it should form the infrastructure on which innovation can be safely scaled.

papers.title: GeoVLDrive: Geometry-Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning for Autonomous Driving

Multi-layer features from a 3D foundation model augment the vision-language backbone through gated cross-attention. A structured latent chain of thought (CoT) organizes future scene geometry, key-agent motion, and meta-actions into ordered, separately supervised latent states. An action expert generates trajectory proposals from these states and multi-layer scene features, and ranks them using scene-grounded, interacting score tokens. We also introduce NAVSIM 3DQA to train and evaluate metric 3D spatial and motion understanding. GeoVLDrive achieves 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. On NAVSIM 3DQA, the geometry-grounded backbone scores 89.2% overall, 4.6 percentage points above the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B baseline. On LingoQA, the backbone achieves 68.6% Lingo-Judge accuracy.

papers.title: Generalizable Feed-Forward 3D Hand-Object Reconstruction with Coarse-to-Fine Contact Estimation

papers.abstract: Reconstructing the 3D poses of hands and objects from a single image, together with the contact between them, is fundamental to understanding manipulation. To be practical, the reconstruction must generalize to unseen objects, and the contact must be localized precisely. Yet joint feed-forward estimators often rely on predefined object sets, while contact is typically predicted from image features alone, without the explicit geometry needed to localize it. To address both limitations, we present HORCRUX, a unified feed-forward transformer with coarse-to-fine contact estimation. For unseen objects, a frozen foundation model encodes the object from a given or image-reconstructed mesh rather than from object-specific knowledge. A shared transformer then reasons jointly over the object and one or two hands to keep them aligned. For precise contact, coarse per-joint predictions from latent features are resolved over finer hand regions using the reconstructed geometry. Across seven benchmarks, HORCRUX achieves state-of-the-art object and hand pose accuracy among joint estimators and outperforms a dedicated contact estimator in fine-grained contact. These results suggest that contact is best estimated jointly with reconstruction, whose geometry directly localizes it.

papers.authors: Tianyuan Yuan, Baijun Ye, Shicheng Cao, Xing Nie, Xiaopeng Yu, Ke Dong, Zijie Zhao, Shenling Qiu, et al.
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generators for robot control by jointly predicting future camera frames and actions, transferring physical priors learned from video into manipulation policies. However, generating future frames before every action makes test-time inference too slow for closed-loop control, while most existing policies remain restricted to short observation histories. Performance scales consistently with pretraining data, with human ego video driving the largest gains in out-of-distribution generalization: G0.7 achieves a 70.8 mean score across five simulation benchmark suites, 48% and 54% zero-shot pick-and-place success on Galaxea R1 Pro and R1 Lite, 96.7% in-distribution and 93.3% out-of-distribution success on video-conditioned in-context learning tasks, and 86.9% mean task progress across seven real-world post-training tasks including multi-minute box folding, drink preparation, and product bagging.

papers.title: From Replacement to Augmentation: A Human-Centered Framework for Consumer Robots
papers.authors: Wangao Cao
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence and related hardware and software technologies have accelerated the development of consumer robots, creating new opportunities for robots to support people in everyday life. However, advanced technology is only the foundation for achieving this goal. A complete design concept for robots aimed at ordinary consumers is also needed. This paper examines the importance of positioning consumer robots as tools for human augmentation, the reason why consumer robot interaction design should mainly use intuitive operation, and the safety issues that influence user trust and acceptance. The analysis argues that consumer robots should prioritize human augmentation rather than complete robot autonomy. This approach protects consumer control while giving users stronger capabilities. In addition, robot products can only be psychologically accepted when consumers trust them. To achieve this positioning, intuitive interaction can reduce the barriers for ordinary consumers and allow more natural interaction. Products should also provide data privacy protection, control-right protection, and safety that can be perceived by users. The significance of this paper is that it provides a consumer-centered design framework for robots aimed at ordinary consumers.

papers.title: From Pixels to Actions: A Comprehensive Review of Spatiotemporal Understanding from Visual Perception to Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to perceive, reconstruct, reason about, predict, and act within dynamic three-dimensional environments, is a unifying goal for robotics, autonomous driving, and embodied AI. Existing surveys treat its components, from video language models to Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, in isolation, obscuring how progress at one capability carries over to the next. This review provides a unified, critical analysis of the full pipeline from pixels to actions. We introduce the Pixels-to-Actions (P2A) hierarchy, a six-level taxonomy: (L1) visual perception, (L2) temporal perception, (L3) spatial and 4D understanding, (L4) spatiotemporal reasoning, (L5) predictive world modeling, and (L6) embodied action. For each level, we analyze architectures, spatiotemporal tokenization, multi-sensor inputs, and training paradigms. We examine whether stronger geometric grounding and temporal reasoning translate into better prediction and action, and formalize streaming spatial intelligence as a unifying target. We extend the analysis to medical imaging, remote sensing, AR/VR, surveillance, and digital twins, and compare datasets, benchmarks, and metrics from video question answering to closed-loop evaluation. We distill ten open problems, including weak spatial grounding in multimodal models, limited physical commonsense, costly long-horizon reasoning, fragmented benchmarks, and insufficient safety evaluation. A continuously updated repository of the reviewed literature is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Pixels-to-Actions.

papers.title: Follow-Bench 2.0: An End-to-End 3D Benchmark for Socially-Aware Robot Person Following
papers.authors: Hanjing Ye, Tianle Zeng, Jianwei Peng, Yanci Wen, Yuchen Zhou, Yonggen Ling, Hong Zhang
papers.abstract: Socially-aware robot person following (RPF) requires a mobile robot to follow a designated person in dynamic human environments while maintaining target identity, avoiding obstacles and pedestrians, and preserving socially comfortable formations. Existing benchmarks only partially evaluate this coupled problem: embodied visual tracking benchmarks emphasize target visibility with limited social interaction, person re-identification benchmarks study perception without closed-loop control, and motion-planning benchmarks often assume ground-truth target and pedestrian states. We introduce Follow-Bench 2.0, an end-to-end 3D benchmark for evaluating socially-aware RPF under coupled perception--planning challenges. Built in Unreal Engine, Follow-Bench 2.0 provides difficulty-leveled scenarios with diverse pedestrian flows, lighting and weather conditions, cluttered layouts, bottlenecks, queueing behaviors, distractors, and temporary target occlusions. The benchmark supports modular perception--planning pipelines, end-to-end visual policies, and foundation-model-based active trackers under a unified closed-loop protocol. It further evaluates both back- and side-following configurations and reports safety--comfort metrics covering task success, target visibility, target recovery, social-space intrusion, following formation, and motion smoothness. Experiments show that RPF-oriented modular pipelines substantially outperform current end-to-end visual policies on close and socially comfortable following, but also reveal that socially-aware RPF remains far from solved in interaction-heavy environments and especially in side-following. Follow-Bench 2.0 therefore provides a diagnostic platform for studying how perception errors, occlusions, crowd interactions, and following configurations jointly affect robot person following.

papers.title: Fast Muscle-Driven Whole-Body Motion Tracking with a Differentiable World Model
papers.authors: Kaibo He, Maciej Bakowicz, Shihe Zhou, Yusen Feng, Yanan Sui, Dhanush Radhakrishnan
papers.abstract: Tracking motion capture with a whole-body musculoskeletal model means coordinating hundreds of muscles through contact, and current controllers take hours to days of GPU time to train, so every tuning decision is expensive. SuperMimic trains a tracking policy by backpropagating through the rollouts of a learned world model. We extend it to MS-Human-700 (700 muscles) and MyoFullBody (354 muscles), with MuJoCo's activation dynamics inside the world model. To make its training fast, our recipe takes the speedups developed for the Unitree G1, replaces three of their settings that fail on muscles, and adds four changes of our own: observations without muscle geometry, data collection concurrent with the updates, Beta exploration noise that keeps every excitation in $[0,1]$, and 50 Hz control. On one RTX 5090 it trains MS-Human-700 in 6.3 minutes to the held-out return that SuperMimic's published hyperparameters reach in 3.9 hours, 37$\times$ sooner, and in 20 minutes to lower tracking errors than theirs after 10 hours. It trains MyoFullBody 34$\times$ sooner without retuning. Ablations show what is specific to muscles: a higher policy learning rate stalls half of the runs, and clipped Gaussian noise adds a tonic co-contraction that Beta noise avoids. Finally, refining the policy's actions through the world model at test time lowers the position error by a further 26% with no held-out clip failing, and reaches the same return after 5.1 instead of 6.3 minutes of training. Code, the training recipe and videos are on the project page https://muscle-supermimic.beanpow.top.

papers.title: FOCI: Trajectory Optimization on Gaussian Splats for Gaussian Robots
papers.authors: Mario Gomez Andreu, Carlos Martinez Cuenca, Maximum Wilder-Smith, Victor Klemm, Vaishakh Patil, Marco Hutter, Jesus Tordesillas
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently gained popularity as a faster alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis methods. Leveraging the spatial information encoded in 3DGS, this work proposes FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), an algorithm that is able to optimize trajectories directly on the Gaussians themselves. FOCI leverages a novel and interpretable collision formulation for 3DGS using the notion of the overlap integral between Gaussians. The formulation presented applies to different robot morphologies (e.g., fixed and mobile base manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and handles both static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments. Contrary to other approaches, which represent the robot with conservative bounding boxes that underestimate the traversability of the environment, we propose to represent the environment and the robot as Gaussian Splats. This not only has desirable computational properties, but also allows for orientation-aware planning, allowing the robot to pass through very tight and narrow spaces. We extensively test our algorithm in both synthetic and real Gaussian Splats, showcasing that collision-free trajectories for legged, aerial and manipulator robots can be computed in seconds, even with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians making up the environment. The code is available at https://github.com/leggedrobotics/foci

papers.title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
papers.authors: Kshitiz, Zheyuan Hu, Robyn Wu, Yizhou Li, Yunchu Zhang, Vattanary Tevy, Kavya Tayal, Shawn Yin, et al.
papers.abstract: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $β$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.

papers.title: EviCraft: Can Minecraft Agents Find What They Cannot See?
papers.authors: Wenyou Yi, Lantian Zhang, Guanlin Chen, Xingqiu Xu, Haiyang Sun, Minrui Huang, Tianle Liang, Hao Chen, et al.
papers.abstract: In Minecraft, a common testbed for embodied agents, semantic tools such as mineBlock pick targets from the simulator's loaded world state without a visibility test, so a buried ore the agent has never seen is one call away, and scores cannot show whether the agent searched. We formalize the missing requirement as evidence closure: every decision of an agent system, including those inside its tools, may depend on the world only through facts for which the agent holds evidence. EviCraft is a runtime and benchmark that enforces closure below the agent and makes the admission rule an experimental variable: a perception-grounded regime (G) admits only what is in line of sight or returned by the agent's own actions, and a loaded-state regime (L) reproduces standard tool stacks, with agents, tools, and worlds held fixed. On Survival, the regime effect exceeds the strongest agent's lead: under G, three mid-sized agents reach the diamond in 32%-40% of runs, against 76%-94% under L, and the strongest agent under G scores below each of them under L. In two models, removing only the line-of-sight test closes 93%-96% of the score gap, and loading state only inside tools recovers 70%-98%, so safeguards on observations and queries leave most of the leak open. In open-ended acquisition, the gain from L concentrates in items that depend on buried resources or mobs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/AllenReder/EviCraft

papers.title: EmbodiedStudio: A Task-Driven Simulation Generation Platform for Embodied Learning and Evaluation
papers.authors: Yang Zhao, Xubo Yang
papers.abstract: Training and evaluating robots across diverse tasks requires a supply of simulation environments suited to those tasks. While recent scene and task generators offer a promising way to expand this supply, delivering a usable task environment still faces two practical gaps: generated scenes that look plausible in appearance often fail to support the intended task interactions or remain physically stable in simulation, and generated scoring programs frequently attempt task conditions without implementing them faithfully. We present EmbodiedStudio, a task-driven simulation generation platform that bridges these gaps by jointly authoring scene, task, robot-behavior, and rubric programs under closed-loop simulation feedback and independent review. Crucially, as the coding agent iteratively debugs scenes, behaviors, and stateful rubrics in simulation, this closed-loop process natively yields both forward construction experience for learning to build environments and physical execution experience for policy learning, all bound to frozen environment revisions for repeatable evaluation. Across scene generation, rubric evaluation, ablations, and learning studies, EmbodiedStudio substantially improves task readiness and rubric faithfulness while improving physical stability and retaining actionable supervision signals for layout authoring and policy adaptation.

papers.title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies
papers.authors: Xuanchen Liu, Hejun Zhang, Boxuan Dong, Ying Wu, Heshuai Li, Wen Gao, Yonghong Tian, Weihao Yu
papers.abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $π_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.

papers.title: Embodied AI
papers.authors: Bohan Zhou
papers.abstract: This project investigates embodied artificial intelligence for visual grounding, spatial reasoning, task planning, robot skill coordination, and task-progress estimation. It combines existing research datasets with simulation-generated robot interactions and controlled real-robot experiments where applicable. Research data include RGB and RGB-D images or videos, camera calibration and geometric annotations, natural-language instructions, robot states and action trajectories, scene graphs, planning traces, task outcomes, and derived progress or reward annotations. These data support the development and evaluation of vision-language models, robotic policies, and progress estimators. The project will also generate source code, processing scripts, experiment configurations, selected model checkpoints, evaluation results, and documentation. Data management will support reproducibility while respecting source licences, privacy requirements, and applicable collaboration agreements.

papers.title: EmbodiSafety: Benchmarking Risk Understanding and Response in Embodied AI
papers.authors: Erfei Cui, Shengjia Zhao, Yan Qin, Kaixuan Wang, Junming Chen, Ping Luo, Tianxing Chen
papers.abstract: Progress in embodied foundation models is largely measured by task success, while the physical safety of their decisions remains underexamined. Safety evaluations centered on rule following and binary judgments do not adequately assess whether embodied models understand environmental hazards and make safe decisions. We introduce EmbodiSafety, comprising 1,092 snapshot tasks and 540 trajectory tasks across 844 visual scenarios to assess safety over short and long horizons. Six response modes cover direct execution, refusal, clarification, constrained execution, autonomous recovery, and human escalation. Distinguishing recovery from human intervention makes the boundary of safe autonomy an explicit evaluation target. Our protocol assesses mode correctness, risk identification, and actionable handling, with complete decision accuracy requiring all applicable checks to pass. Claude-Opus-5.5 achieves the highest complete decision accuracy among reference models, reaching 56.1% on snapshots and 61.5% on trajectories. We further develop a data construction pipeline and curate 40k examples for safety alignment. Supervised training on this corpus raises the complete decision accuracy of Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B.

papers.title: EgoLoAF: Learning Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations with Hand-Object Affordances
papers.authors: Yiming Zeng, Jiangyuxuan Dai, Yuheng Na, Tan Zhu Xuan, Zihan Lin, Xinfang Qi, Shijian Zhang, Chengqi Shi, et al.
papers.abstract: Training humanoid vision-language-action (VLA) models relies heavily on costly real-robot teleoperation. Recent efforts convert egocentric human demonstrations into humanoid training data. However, most methods still require wearable motion trackers and leave important hand-object interaction cues implicit. Many also mix in real-robot teleoperation data for VLA post-training. These dependencies limit scalable data collection, while implicit interaction cues make precise contact harder to learn. To overcome these limitations, we propose EgoLoAF, the first paradigm to derive all training data for humanoid loco-manipulation directly from egocentric demonstrations without wearable motion trackers. We post-train the VLA on the converted data alone, without real-robot teleoperation demonstrations, and use explicit hand-object interaction cues to guide action generation. Specifically, to obtain humanoid action targets, we estimate torso motion from recorded camera poses and reconstruct both hand trajectories from video. From the same recording, we use each hand's current pose relative to the object to represent hand-object affordances. During post-training, we inject these affordances into the action expert through cross-attention while keeping the vision-language backbone frozen. Additionally, we release 128,400 egocentric demonstration episodes spanning 1,000 hours and 1,284 tasks, together with converted humanoid action trajectories and rendered robot-view observations. Across four real-world tasks, EgoLoAF nearly achieves teleoperation performance (73.1 vs. 74.4 in mean Task Progress Score), while achieving a mean 4.03 times improvement in data-collection efficiency.

papers.title: Ego2Real: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Visuo-Tactile Demonstrations
papers.authors: Ange Bao, Haishan Zhang, Lingzi Xie, Shuang Li, Pei Zhao, Ling Shi, Bidan Huang
papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations offers a scalable path toward robot skill acquisition. Vision alone, however, provides limited information about physical contacts and the demonstrator's force intent, leading to ambiguities in interpreting hand-object interactions. Capturing human touch via tactile sensing is therefore crucial for reliable human-to-robot dexterous skill transfer. We present Ego2Real, a framework that leverages egocentric demonstrations and tactile gloves to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to robotic hands. Ego2Real incorporates tactile supervision at two complementary stages: (1) tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction, which uses measured tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry; and (2) contact-informed reinforcement learning, which translates human contact patterns into robotic contact rewards. By combining refined motion references with physical contact rewards during training, Ego2Real guides anthropomorphic robotic hands to emulate demonstrated contact behaviors while adapting to their own morphology and actuation. Experiments show that incorporating tactile supervision into both reconstruction and policy learning yields higher manipulation success rates, underscoring the importance of enriching egocentric demonstrations with tactile observations to improve their quality and transferability.
