papers.title: S-BFM: A Behavioral Foundation Model for Humanoid Control from Sparse Spatiotemporal Goals
papers.authors: Kun Yang, Xuanyu Chen, Jing Tan, Yanjing Liu, Yubo Zhao, Renjing Xu, Addison Lin Wang
papers.abstract: General-purpose whole-body trackers can execute diverse humanoid motions, but they require dense reference trajectories. However, tasks usually specify only where, in which posture, and when the robot should arrive, leaving the motion in between to a separate planner. Inspired by human motor coordination, our key idea is that a low-level controller can organize the intervening motion and its pace by itself from sparse goals with arrival times. In this paper, we propose S-BFM, a novel behavioral foundation model superior in its autonomy: it generates whole-body transitions from target postures, poses, and arrival times alone. Specifically, we first introduce Spatial Grounding, which adds world-frame position and heading to a forward-backward behavior representation through spatial reconstruction. Then, Time-Conditioned Distillation is designed to learn transitions and pace from real motion through closed-loop imitation of a dense-reference teacher. Lastly, Generative Fine-Tuning is introduced to broaden the covered distances and arrival times with a distilled motion generator. In simulation, S-BFM lowers global joint-position error by over 32% relative to the best baseline under fixed and mixed horizons, and raises fixed-goal reach from 43.5% to 74.6% while cutting terminal position error from 1.67 to 0.26 m. We further deploy S-BFM on the full-size AGIBOT A3 humanoid. Sparse spatiotemporal goals thus suffice for natural, well-timed whole-body motion.

papers.title: Robot-assisted versus laparoscopic-assisted radical right hemicolectomy: short-term and 5-year outcomes in 2057 cases
papers.authors: Taiyuan Li, Ruichen Zhou, Penghui He, Yahang Liang, Feng Xiao, Wenjun Hu, Dongning Liu
papers.abstract: Background With the increasing application of robotic surgical systems in the field of gastrointestinal surgery, their technical advantages in achieving precise dissection and stable manipulation have become increasingly evident in clinical practice. This study aims to compare the perioperative outcomes and long-term survival outcomes of robot-assisted radical right hemicolectomy (RA) and laparoscopic-assisted radical right hemicolectomy (LA) for colon cancer.Methods This study is a retrospective analysis; a total of 2057 patients with right-sided colon cancer were enrolled from the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University between 2015 and 2020. No significant differences were observed in baseline characteristics between the two groups. The primary endpoints of this study were 5-year cancer-specific survival (CSS) and disease-free survival (DFS) after surgery, while the secondary endpoints were perioperative outcomes.Results The RA group was associated with significantly higher 5-year CSS and DFS than the LA group (CSS: 79.9% vs. 74.6%, p = 0.005; DFS: 74.2% vs. 67.3%, p = 0.001). Surgical approach was an independent prognostic factor for both CSS and DFS (CSS: hazard ratio (HR) = 0.75, p = 0.008; DFS: HR = 0.75, p = 0.002). For perioperative outcomes, the RA group was associated with less intraoperative blood loss, more lymph nodes harvested (both p < 0.001), and a lower complication rate (p = 0.001).Conclusions RA was associated with more favourable perioperative outcomes and better long-term survival than LA.

papers.title: RoboPRO: A Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-Aware Benchmark for Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Zhiyuan Li, Charles Eret, Dingsheng Liu, Xuan Zhao, Joshua Choi, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, et al.
papers.abstract: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. Project page: https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/

papers.title: RoboDyna: A Benchmark for Evaluating Robotic Manipulation under Physically Grounded Dynamics
papers.authors: Zhiyuan Li, Rui Heng Yang, Xuan Zhao, Amir Rasouli
papers.abstract: Object manipulation in the dynamic real world requires understanding how the environment functions and evolves, and acting accordingly. Existing benchmarks, however, do not adequately address these needs. Physics-oriented benchmarks evaluate predictive fidelity but not closed-loop action. Dynamic robotic manipulation benchmarks often use simplified, physically implausible object motions, limiting evaluation of reasoning and action under realistic dynamics. Evaluation is also typically synchronized, freezing the environment during inference and making computation time irrelevant to task outcomes. To this end, we propose RoboDyna, a benchmark for evaluating the physical understanding and action capabilities of manipulation policies in dynamic scenes. RoboDyna comprises 20 conceptual dynamic tasks spanning five capability categories, with simple objects and minimal scene clutter, under a two-factor difficulty design, and 10 household tasks that instantiate the same capabilities in visually and semantically richer simulated real-world environments. RoboDyna provides 3,500 expert demonstrations, paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocols, metrics for task success and partial completion, and interactive tools for human baseline evaluation. Evaluating vision-language-action models and a world-action model across 5.4K episodes, we find that all policies achieve success rates below 20%, revealing substantial limitations in dynamic manipulation. The world-action model captures simple physical dynamics but struggles with complex interactions, and its prediction fidelity does not consistently align with task success. papers.title: RoboColiseum: Co-evolution of Simulation, Evaluation, and Models
papers.authors: Chenghao Yin, Da Huang, Di Yang, Jichao Wang, Junhui Wu, Nanshu Zhao, Tong Ran, Zhijun Li, et al.

Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.

papers.title: Real-time neuromorphic audio and vision perception for autonomous robotic applications: Integration and experimental evaluation on a rover platform
papers.authors: Guillem Fustier-Castillo, Ruben Ribes-Serrano, Javier Naranjo-Alcazar, Vicent Ortiz-Castello, Pedro Zuccarello
papers.abstract: Neuromorphic sensing and computing offer a promising alternative to conventional deep learning pipelines for mobile robots, where perception must run continuously under tight latency and energy constraints. However, most neuromorphic solutions are still evaluated offline or on isolated benchmarks, and their integration into complete robotic systems remains largely unexplored. In this technical report, a four-wheel rover platform is presented that combines three real-time perception pipelines: a classical audio tagging pipeline based on Pretrained Audio Neural Networks (PANNs) running on an NVIDIA Jetson GPU, a neuromorphic audio pipeline in which a spiking neural network (SNN) is deployed on the SynSense Xylo Audio~2 chip, and a neuromorphic vision pipeline in which events from an event-based camera are processed by the SpikeYOLO spiking detector for traffic cone detection. On the Xylo chip, the whole processing chain---from the microphone signal to the classification of low- and high-pitched sounds---is performed on-chip, while the host only configures the device and reads the output neurons. All models are deployed as containerised services and integrated through ROS~2, and a configurable action dispatcher maps the detected classes to robot behaviours, closing the loop between perception and actuation. The platform is demonstrated in a proof-of-concept scenario in which the robot reacts to sound classes detected by both audio pipelines and detects traffic cones with the event camera, showing the feasibility of integrating neuromorphic hardware into a multimodal robotic platform operating in real time.

papers.title: ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models
papers.authors: Zhaochen Guo, Yunke Wang, Siyu Xu, Zijian Wang, Chenghao Xia, Chengbin Du, Shinan Liu, Chang Xu
papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.

We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.

papers.title: Probing Invisible Actuation Shifts for Test-time Calibration of Visuomotor Policies
papers.authors: Jie Liu, Hui Xie, Qinfeng Feng, Joaquin Vanschoren
papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) are increasingly deployed on robots whose cameras and controllers differ from those used to collect their training data. Such deployment introduces two kinds of shifts. Visual shifts, such as a moved camera, change the observed images; actuation shifts, such as a retuned controller, latency or an added payload, change only how commanded actions translate into robot motion. Invisible to the policy, actuation shifts sharply degrade its success, even under domain randomization. In this work, we propose PEA, a test-time calibration method that identifies actuation shifts through active probing before task execution. Specifically, before each episode, the robot executes a short probe that moves one arm axis at a time with known commands, so that gain, delay and drift leave separable traces. A closed-form identifier estimates them from the response, and PEA compensates every subsequent command so that the robot executes the motion the policy intends. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts. Experiments on LIBERO with a WAM and a VLA show that, without any policy training, the identifier of PEA recovers most of the success lost to actuation shifts and generalizes to shifts unseen during training (e.g., from 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy).

papers.abstract: How does future prediction affect context-dependent robot control? We introduce PonderPounce-WM, extending PonderPounce with three future tokens supervised to predict visual-feature changes. Its pretrained MLLM, Ponder, integrates history and demonstrations into continuous cognition for the action model, Pounce. We investigate token ordering and delivery to distinguish predictive supervision from direct future conditioning. On RoboMME, cognition-first ordering with cognition-only delivery improves success from 60.83% to 67.42%. With the same ordering, direct future-token delivery yields 64.00% success. Probes show increased future information in cognition while the tested past-event attributes remain largely decodable. Across four real-robot tasks, PonderPounce-WM achieves 67.44% mean success under asynchronous execution, compared with 60.98% for PonderPounce. These results suggest that future prediction can improve context-dependent control through auxiliary supervision without delivering future tokens to the action model.

papers.title: PACE: Policy Augmentation and Compensation With Explicit Disturbance Estimation for Robust Locomotion
papers.authors: Shixuan Han, Yuyang Wang, Jingting Jia, Zeshuai Chen, Jindou Jia, Kexin Guo, Xiang Yu
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has made quadrupedal locomotion remarkably robust. To handle unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances, domain randomization is usually employed to make a policy hedge against every condition it might meet. However, maintaining accurate tracking across varying dynamics and generalizing beyond the sampled range remain challenging. Here we show that explicitly estimating the disturbance and feeding the resulting estimation back into both the policy and the controller can relax this compromise. We introduce Policy Augmentation and Compensation with Explicit disturbance estimation (PACE). The framework lumps payload variations, center-of-mass (CoM) shifts, actuator degradation, and external forces into one joint-space disturbance. A nonlinear observer subsequently recovers this disturbance online without requiring joint acceleration measurements. The disturbance estimation provides feedforward torque compensation as the foundational control pathway and further augments the policy observation to enable disturbance-aware action generation. Considering the learning difficulty of fast-varying contact effects, we further provide an analytical contact estimation approach from joint and inertial measurements, without demanding force sensors. Across eleven simulated dynamics conditions, PACE reduces velocity-tracking error by 18.1% to 57.0% against state-of-the-art baselines, and maintains improved tracking under out-of-distribution (OOD) commands. Notably, in real-world experiments, the deployed real robot carried an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass. It also negotiated unseen 16 cm step-downs and crossed five outdoor terrains. The policy was trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation with at most 3 kg of added mass.

papers.title: PACE-WM: Parallel World Modeling with Action History for Visual Planning
papers.authors: Haishan Liu, Shijie Lian, Bin Yu, Yao Zhang, Changti Wu, Fanping Liu, Jianzheng Liu, Lei Xie, et al.
papers.abstract: JEPA-style world models support visual planning by predicting future representations conditioned on future actions. However, similar observations can conceal different motion states, making temporal context essential for interpreting future action effects. We propose PACE-WM, a parallel world model that uses executed-action history to contextualize future prediction and planning. Specifically, PACE-WM maintains a recurrent memory of executed actions and uses this memory to condition a causal Transformer. PACE-WM predicts multiple future representations in parallel without recursive predicted-state feedback within each prediction window. We further introduce Reference-Anchored Minimum Progress (RAMP) for action selection during planning. RAMP scores candidate actions by their predicted goal improvement along direct and split paths relative to a shared reference. Across four visual planning tasks, PACE-WM with RAMP achieves an average success rate of $98\%$ and plans approximately $7$-$9\times$ faster than autoregressive LeWM under matched CEM settings. We also construct four controlled benchmarks to evaluate PACE-WM's capabilities in motion disambiguation, goal-relative motion, and goal adaptation. Project page is available at https://github.com/LHS180/PACE-WM.

papers.title: Opto-Electronic Hybrid Reinforcement Learning Based on MZI for Robotic Manipulator Control
papers.authors: Mengting Yu, Shuiying Xiang, Changjian Xie, Yonghang Chen, Haowen Zhao, Xingxing Guo, Zhijian Hao, Yahui Zhang, et al.
papers.abstract: Precise motion control for autonomous robots is a core technical enabler for the large-scale deployment of embodied intelligence. In particular, basic manipulation tasks, such as point-to-point reaching and target grasping with robotic manipulators, impose stringent requirements on control accuracy, real-time response, and energy efficiency for edge deployment. As a prevailing end-to-end control paradigm, reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable capabilities in autonomous learning and generalization for decision-making in continuous action spaces. Nevertheless, constrained by electronic computing architectures, it generally suffers from substantial computing overhead, high inference latency and limited energy efficiency, making low-power edge deployment challenging. Optical computing, benefiting from its high-speed parallelism, offers a promising route to break energy-efficiency bottlenecks; however, research on the integration of optical computing and RL remains at an early stage. In this work, we propose a Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI)-based opto-electronic hybrid RL architecture. We adopted two algorithm structures: Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient combined with Hindsight Experience Replay (DDPG-HER) and Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient combined with HER (TD3-HER). We implemented the key layer linear computation of the spiking neural network (SNN) Actor on an optical MZI chip for the reaching task of a Franka Emika Panda robotic manipulator. The architecture is evaluated in the PyBullet simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves an energy efficiency of 1.39 TOPS/W and an inference latency of 120ps while maintaining control accuracy, which provide a feasible pathway toward energy-efficient and precise control for robots.

papers.title: Not Coded Dopamine: What Would Count as a Machine That Feels
papers.authors: Abdelrahman El Sayad
papers.abstract: In July 2026 I spent two days asking a large language model to find me a sentient machine I could put into a robot, and I rejected every answer it gave. This paper turns that rejection into a test. A system earns the right to be discussed as a candidate for feeling only if it meets four conditions. It must be embodied, sensing and acting through a body of its own. It must run a homeostatic economy with real stakes, in which internal variables have to be held in range for the system to go on existing, and in which the system itself does the holding. It must contain no labeled shortcuts: no component may carry the name of a feeling or a drive unless removing that component removes the function the name describes. And it must persist, carrying its state and its history forward in time without a human reloading it. I score the current candidate builds against these conditions: a vision language action model on a robot arm, spiking neural networks, a whole connectome simulation in a toy robot, living neuron cultures and brain organoids, and fungal computing, including hybrids where the record supports them, with the fungal hybrid examined in depth. None passes. I then state the harder problem plainly. No accepted test for machine consciousness exists, so passing my four conditions would not prove inner experience either. The conditions are gates for taking a claim seriously. They are not a detector. I close with the observations that would change my mind.

papers.title: NormFlowSDE: Normalizing Flows for Amortized Bayesian State Estimation
papers.authors: Yi Zhang, Lars Mikelsons
papers.abstract: Bayesian state estimators, such as Kalman filters, estimate states from noisy observations based on dynamical models. However, obtaining accurate models can be challenging when the system involves effects that are difficult to model faithfully, such as friction, impacts, and deformation in contact-rich manipulation. Uncertainty in system parameters, inputs, and disturbances, together with simplified noise models, can further introduce simulation-to-reality mismatch and degrade estimation accuracy. These limitations motivate learning a distribution over state trajectories conditioned on observations and controls without explicitly specifying the underlying physical models. We introduce NormFlowSDE, an amortized Bayesian state estimator that learns a distribution over state trajectories by combining neural stochastic differential equations with conditional normalizing flows. Its key design choice is to utilize the capability of normalizing flows to learn stochastic behavior of variables, while leveraging the continuous-time dynamics of SDEs to model the evolution of states over time. Once trained, the model draws state paths for new measurement sequences without per-sequence optimization. In addition, we connect NormFlowSDE to stochastic continuous-time dynamics by proving weak convergence of a mean-centered, drift-corrected inference scheme to an Itô diffusion under stated assumptions. Finally, we benchmark NormFlowSDE against direct estimators and learned particle filters based on normalizing flows on partially observed dynamical systems, including simulated systems and real-world robot datasets. The results show that NormFlowSDE attains the lowest estimation error with calibrated uncertainty intervals on both robot datasets and filters four times faster than the fastest particle filter on every dataset.

papers.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration: Turning Field Anomalies into Simulation Fine-Tuning
papers.authors: Youwei Yu, Lantao Liu
papers.abstract: A policy that transfers from simulation to a lab robot often fails in the field. Calibrating a simulator from real-world data typically targets only a few hand-picked parameters, and even calibrated simulators fail to capture unmodeled dynamics, while environments reconstructed via onboard perception inherit sensing noise and artifacts. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a framework based on conditional flow matching that infers online, directly from a robot's execution data, both simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity - the remaining dynamics discrepancy and the gap between perceived and true environment geometry. A simulation-trained anomaly detector determines when recalibration or fine-tuning is required using onboard sensory signals alone, while an exploration policy actively modulates posterior uncertainty using optimism in the face of uncertainty. Across five robot platforms with up to 39 calibrated parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain map, NFC achieves the most accurate posterior distributions compared to established simulation-based inference baselines. In physical outdoor experiments with a wheeled robot suffering an axle failure across snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC increases rough-terrain navigation success from 26% to 70% while reducing orientation jerk by 88%.

papers.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
papers.authors: Youwei Yu, Lantao Liu
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. papers.title: NavTTT: Adaptive Parametric Memory via Hierarchical Test-Time Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.authors: Xiaoyu Luo, Chengxing Lin, Jiaxin Huang, Jiale Liu, Jingyu Guo, Sirui Chen, Aolin Li, Shaoli Huang, et al.
papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

papers.title: NavRSI: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.authors: Guangzhao Dai, Guoxin Lian, Shuo Wang, Shengbin Yue, Qianru Sun, Xiangbo Shu, Bin Zhu
papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM-environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability.

MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Unified Proximity-Tactile Observation by a Capacitive Fingertip Array Constrained by a Metal Phalanx
papers.authors: Shun Cheng
papers.abstract: A capacitive fingertip array on a metal phalanx under thin silicone skin senses centimetre-scale conductive targets by fringing fields and contact force by dielectric compression. Electrode-to-body parasitics exceed the useful proximity increment by one to three orders of magnitude, and crosstalk and time-division-multiplexing (TDM) settling prevent identifying the capacitance-to-digital converter (CDC) reading with the electrode-target capacitance. The array is modelled as a multi-conductor system (sensing electrodes, driven-shield nodes, phalanx ground and an external target). The CDC measurand follows from the Maxwell capacitance matrix, with each inactive termination in the observation operator. Three mechanisms are examined: driven-shield hiding of shield-branch current and gain/phase-mismatch leakage; distinct far- and near-field operators; and TDM settling as a frame-rate limit set by shield load. A single layer used for both proximity and force reads Delta C = Delta C_force + Delta C_dielectric(epsilon_target), so its force map cannot be material-independent. A dual-array stack is analysed: the outer array is grounded as a Faraday screen during contact, and the inner array reads silicone-gap compression. FEM simulations give a monotonic, nonlinear contact response (4.6 fF at 0.05 mm to 370 fF at 0.5 mm on a 1.08 pF base), a nylon-versus-metal difference of at most 0.3 fF at exported-matrix resolution (not mesh-converged), mutual-term cancellation under driven-shield readout, and about 1 fF crosstalk on the coarse mesh. In proximity mode, electrode-shield coupling of 1.47 pF makes 10^{-3}-10^{-4} mismatch a quantitative gate: a 15.9 fF increment at 5 mm equals the leakage at |epsilon_A| ~ 10^{-2}. Force map, mechanical crosstalk and all bench quantities remain unvalidated; the equations and FEM evidence are a baseline for prototype calibration, not measured performance claims.

As deposited materials shift, sag, accumulate, or behave unexpectedly, designers may need to interpret changing conditions and decide whether, when, and how to intervene during fabrication. While some research has begun to explore AI support for additive manufacturing, less is known about how people should interact with AI during unfolding, materially consequential processes. This creates a need to explore interaction models that support situated judgement and negotiation among people, AI systems, machines, and materials. In this half-day workshop, we ask the OzCHI community: how might AI support human decision-making as robotic 3D printing processes unfold? Participants will explore this question through speculative activities that progress from hands-on collaborative making to simulated AI assistance and to a low-fidelity enactment of a robotic 3D-printing scenario. Rather than testing a working AI system, the session uses speculative role-play as a design probe to examine how people interpret, question, reject, and build on AI suggestions as material conditions evolve. Workshop insights will be synthesised into a preliminary vocabulary of interaction patterns and communication needs to inform the design of future AI-assisted fabrication interfaces and workflows.

Primary outcomes were right-wrist force, jerk and angle in the lower-calyx phase; others were exploratory, analysed with participant-level Welch tests, Hedges g, 95% CIs, Holm correction and a mixed model for group × phase interaction. Results Procedure time was longer in novices (115.5 vs 61.5 s). In the lower-calyx phase, novices showed higher right-wrist force (1.87 vs 1.16 N; Holm p = 0.026), jerk (Holm p = 0.020) and angle (31.6° vs 24.9°; Holm p = 0.026), with no upper-calyx differences; force and jerk showed significant group × phase interactions (p = 0.004, 0.007) but angle did not (p = 0.35). Force, jerk and dispersion correlated strongly with movement speed (ρ = 0.93–0.99), and group differences were attenuated after speed adjustment. Conclusion In this simulator study, experience-related differences in estimated wrist load emerged mainly during lower-calyx access, whereas wrist angle differed throughout, pinpointing an ergonomic target. Because estimates were kinematics-derived and not EMG-validated, findings are hypothesis-generating; correlating them with physiological muscle activity is an important next step for robot-assisted ureteroscopy design.

papers.title: Many Plans at Once: Diverse Top-Quality Planning in Continuous Time
papers.authors: Mahyar Jahani-nasab, Hamid Rezatofighi, Mor Vered, Buser Say
papers.abstract: Planners for physical systems usually return a single trajectory, which leaves no alternative when an unmodeled constraint invalidates the chosen route or downstream preferences change. A set of plans computed in advance provides ready-made alternatives and warm-starts for fast adaptation, but only if the plans are both low-cost and mutually distinct. Discrete planning addresses this with top-quality and diverse planning, but these ideas do not transfer to continuous time, where every valid trajectory has infinitely many valid near-copies, and existing trajectory planners converge to one or a few solutions. We present Many Plans at Once (MPAO), which treats every plan it finds as a reason to search elsewhere: it samples untrained neural networks whose outputs meet the boundary conditions by construction, trains corrections shared by networks from the same distribution, stores every validated plan, and adapts its sampling to what it has found, which makes it anytime. We define the goal by bringing the cost bound of top-quality planning and the distinctness threshold of diverse planning to continuous time. Under equal budgets against five baselines, MPAO is the only method that solves all 40 instances across four domains. On contact-rich manipulation, it is the only method with plans within 25% of the best known cost on one task, and returns about ten times as many such plans as the strongest baseline on the other two.

papers.title: ManipScope: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Instruction Following and Generalization in Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Jiacheng Li, Yaping Li, Congsheng Xu, Qingchen Liu, Haonan Wang, Zhijie Deng, Jiahu Qin
papers.abstract: Completing a manipulation task does not establish that a robot follows the requested goal rather than a familiar routine. ManipScope is an evaluation-only diagnostic benchmark for robotic instruction following under changed task requirements. Built on RoboTwin 2.0's simulation resources, it specifies 48 held-out scenes across six task families with explicit source-task links; policies are trained on unmodified RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrations, and no demonstrations of the scenes are provided, so success requires reusing skills under a changed request rather than fitting supplied examples. Beyond task success, ManipScope provides a chain of diagnostics in which each step tests one explanation of a failure. For twelve policy checkpoints, 84.6% of failures in 13,200 episodes on eleven selection scenes displace a distractor, and gripper records show that failed episodes usually grasp a non-target. When the target is reassigned among the candidates on identical initial states, ten checkpoints follow every instruction on 3.9% of 1,000 states, below the 16% of an instruction-blind chooser, while a GPT-6 agent run as positive control reaches 88%. The failure recurs on unmodified training tasks and is not explained by missing manipulation skills, so success in these scenes largely reflects instruction-independent preferences; two checkpoints trained on the same data nevertheless follow color instructions. In a feasibility test, letting an agent select the target and the policy execute partly restores instruction following. Case studies with future-video and internal-intervention probes further show that forecasts and execution can agree on the wrong target and that action changes need not transfer the goal. Success, consistency, and sensitivity must each be checked against the requested goal.

papers.title: LiDAR Signals for Robot Locomotion: Spherical Range Images Enable Robust Sim-to-Real Transfer
papers.authors: Nian Liu, Xinyi Tong, Ming Ren, Long Ye, Zhaofeng He
papers.abstract: Existing legged-locomotion systems commonly rely on depth images or online elevation maps. However, depth-based policies suffer from perceptual sim-to-real discrepancies due to imperfect depth sensor modeling, while map-based approaches are vulnerable to drift and misalignment. LiDAR offers direct measurements of the surrounding geometry, but raw LiDAR scans lack a compact, structured representation for high-frequency control. We propose a LiDAR perception pipeline that maintains perceptual consistency across simulation and reality through sensing- and representation-level alignment. At the sensor level, we recover frame-wise angular sampling patterns from the physical LiDAR and replay them in simulation with GPU ray casting. At the representation level, simulated and real returns undergo the same spherical range image encoding, yielding a fixed-size policy observation for end-to-end training and direct deployment without teacher--student distillation, online elevation mapping, or adaptation. Experiments show that our range-image policies achieve stronger sim-to-real transfer than depth- and elevation-map-based baselines, while ablations confirm the importance of the proposed sensing components. More visualizations and real-world videos are available at the \href{https://lidar-img.github.io/}

papers.title: Learning from Incomplete Actions: Interval Motion Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.authors: Yunpeng Mei, Chenyu Wang, Xiaowen Zhu, Chenbo Xin, Hongjie Cao, Yiyuan Li, Chengye Zhang, YuAn Wang, et al.
papers.abstract: Visual labeling of egocentric demonstrations often leaves contiguous gaps in action supervision. Reliable poses around a gap still provide its net translation and rotation. We use this information to train vision-language-action policies while preserving ordinary flow matching on reliable local actions. A composition objective constrains the aggregate motion of missing-action estimates, combining multiple fixed windows when a gap exceeds the policy horizon. A shared interval branch learns from reliable endpoints and supplies the composition target. On LIBERO with 20% of demonstrations and 70.5% missing actions, the main method achieves 87.9% mean success over three training runs. In one paired comparison with matched observation exposure and training cost, its advantage over masking is 10.5%. On Ego-informed RoboTwin gaps, success is 45.4%, versus 40.3% for masking. On five real-robot tasks, mean success is 59.6%, versus 54.8% for interval flow matching alone and 48.8% for masking.

papers.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
papers.authors: Inkyu Sa, Gaurav Kuppa, Steve Van der Hoeven, Konstantin Stulov, Rajat Bhageria, Luis Rayas
papers.abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.

papers.title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
papers.authors: Aasheesh Singh, Vishal Vaddina
papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

papers.title: Learning Interaction Dynamics via Motion-Region Guidance for Robotic Video World Models
papers.authors: Yongkang He, Xiaofen Xing, Xiangmin Xu
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.

papers.title: Latent Jacobian Steer: Eliciting Contact-Rich Out-of-Distribution Behaviors from Pretrained Humanoid Controllers
papers.authors: S K Swaminathan, Shivam Sood, Shreyansh Kansal, Chengyang He, Guillaume Adrien Sartoretti
papers.abstract: Given a pretrained general latent-conditioned whole-body humanoid controller, say a behavioral foundation model (BFM), how can we elicit complex and contact-rich out-of-distribution behaviors? Raw joint-action exploration enables direct, task-specific adjustments but can disrupt coordination learned by the pretrained controller, whereas latent exploration retains that coordination but is difficult to steer toward desired physical effects. To combine the complementary strengths of these exploration spaces, we propose Latent Jacobian Steer (LJS), which couples sampling in direct joint-action space with the semantics of the learned frozen controller's input latent space. For a task specified through desired physical effects, we sample task-relevant joint-action perturbations and map them through a damped local inverse of the policy Jacobian to obtain candidate latent ($z$) commands. These commands are executed through the frozen pretrained policy, while exploration is directed toward the physical outcomes required by the new task. Candidate outcomes are evaluated in simulation and composed into latent-command sequences that accomplish the task. Ablations show that neither action-space nor latent-space exploration alone provides the same capability as their coupling. Across diverse out-of-distribution tasks, simulation-based searching using this method produces contact-rich behaviors, including hurdling, manipulating articulated objects, and opening doors through non-prehensile contact. Over ten seeds, LJS completes more of each humanoid task than when searching in either space alone. Beyond humanoids, it also steers a goal-conditioned dexterous hand policy through four assembly tasks better than searching in goal space directly.

papers.title: LCA of smart building energy systems and installations from a Nordic perspective
papers.authors: Bojana Petrovic, Marianne Kjendseth Wiik, Lina Morkūnaitė, Susana G. Sanfelix, Shahab Zangi, Andrea Ferrantelli, Eduard Petlenkov, Ali Reza Yaghoubi
papers.abstract: The upcoming revision of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) will require reporting of the whole life-cycle global warming potential (GWP) for new buildings from 2028 at the European level. In the Nordic countries, several frontrunners have already introduced national climate declaration requirements for new buildings. The focus was primarily on embodied emissions from building materials. However, buildings also comprise a wide range of building energy systems (BES) and technical installations, which contribute to the overall impact. Despite their importance, there is currently a lack of research regarding these building components. Therefore, this paper presents greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of BES and technical installations by using GWP-total climate data. The embodied GHG emissions from the production of air handling units (AHU), lighting systems, cables, cable joints/connectors, LED kits, panel radiators, and transformers are presented as minimum, median, mean, and maximum values. The analysis is based on a dataset of 1,622 environmental product declarations (EPDs) collected across the Nordic countries. The dataset is largely composed of products manufactured in Sweden (44%), followed by Norway (22%) and Estonia (19%), with smaller shares from Finland (7%), Denmark (6%), and Lithuania (2%). The mean values can be used by building designers and environmental consultants as generic climate data to support early-stage sustainable building design and to address data gaps where product-specific information is unavailable.

papers.title: Knowing What You Carry: Scalable Physics-Anchored World Models for Robotic Planning with Liquid Payloads
papers.authors: Yicheng Zhu, Linfeng Tian, Yang Chen, Tao Li, Zilin Bian
papers.abstract: Payload-carrying robots, such as delivery robots and autonomous trucks, must choose motions that keep them and their payload safe, so their planners predict the outcome of each candidate motion. Modern planners compare thousands of candidates per step on a GPU, using world models such as batched simulators or learned predictors. Most of them assume a rigid payload, but a liquid payload keeps moving after a maneuver, and its state is rarely measured. Near a safety limit, small prediction errors can make an unsafe plan look safe. Coupled fluid simulations are accurate but too costly for every candidate, while low-order slosh models are cheap but accurate only away from resonance. We study this trade-off on a ground vehicle with a partly filled tank near its rollover limit. First, we build PLiMB (Parallel Liquid-MultiBody), a GPU-parallel slosh simulator that, to our knowledge, couples FLIP liquid two-way with many multibody vehicles for the first time. It provides training data and a high-fidelity reference. Second, we propose a scalable physics-anchored world model that combines a modal-slosh and roll prior, an estimate of the hidden liquid state from the vehicle's own motion history (no sensor in the tank), and a learned correction. Without simulating the fluid, it scores thousands of candidate plans in one batched pass within a 20 Hz control tick on one GPU. We judge each world model by the plans it leads a planner to choose. Near the rollover limit, planners that treat the liquid as a rigid payload or use published low-order slosh models repeatedly pick unsafe plans when a safe one exists. Ours never does in our standard tank and makes about half as many in a wide tank whose sloshing mode lies in the maneuver band. There, the liquid state left by earlier driving can change the best plan, and reading it from the vehicle's history halves our model's near-limit prediction error.

papers.title: Joint Optimization of Fleet Size, Localization Infrastructure, and Trajectories for Multi-AUV Persistent Monitoring
papers.authors: Jan Mikołajczyk, Jakub Bałenkowski, Maciej Borowiecki, Jan Ciecierski, Marcel Kolecki, Julian Maleta, Maksymilian Bernacki
papers.abstract: Persistent monitoring of large-scale subsea infrastructure, such as offshore wind farm foundations, export cables, and inspection corridors, remains a fundamental challenge for autonomous underwater systems. The problem is not solely spatial coverage, but rather temporal coverage: ensuring that all relevant regions of interest are revisited within bounded time intervals under limited sensing, navigation uncertainty, and constrained vehicle resources. We compare three classes of trajectory strategies: (1) deterministic lane-based coverage (lawnmower patterns), (2) stochastic exploration (biased random walk with boundary constraints), and (3) coordinated partition-based strategies (Voronoi tessellation). Rather than seeking a universally superior method, we evaluate how varying levels of localization accuracy impact temporal coverage across two distinct operational profiles: persistent monitoring of the entire operational workspace versus targeted inspection of critical infrastructure. We present a simulation-based, quantitatively grounded study of temporal coverage in multi-AUV persistent monitoring, disentangling three interacting design dimensions: (i) trajectory generation strategy, (ii) fleet size, and (iii) localization accuracy provided by fixed acoustic beacon infrastructure. We introduce a cost-aware evaluation framework combining fleet size, number of beacons, and mission energy expenditure into a unified cost function. Results demonstrate that beyond a certain accuracy threshold, improvements in localization yield diminishing returns compared to coordinated trajectory design, an effect often obscured in integrated navigation-planning approaches. Coordinated-partition trajectories enable a reduced fleet size to achieve superior temporal coverage at a 39-46% lower overall life-cycle cost than rigid deterministic paths unoptimized for the localization infrastructure.

papers.title: Iontronic triboelectric tele-perception enabled by ion-relaxation engineering and a lightweight 1D-CNN decoder
papers.authors: Jiaxin Guo, Yan Du, Zhong Lin Wang, Di Wei
papers.abstract: Robots must recognize what is approaching before they touch it. Triboelectric tele-perception meets this need, but its responses stay pinned to the material permittivity (dielectric constant) of the target: the voltage waveform collapses to a scaled copy of the electrostatic coupling, and material identity must then be recovered from a handful of amplitudes. We show that ionic relaxation in an iontronic dielectric breaks this constraint. Dispersing room temperature ionic liquid of BMIMTFSI (10 wt%) in thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) gives an iontronic triboelectric sensor (ITS) whose mobile ions relax on the time scale of an approach event, so that ionic polarization and electrostatic induction act as two independent contributions to the same voltage transient. The resulting waveforms differ in shape, not merely in height: the iontronic film retains 91.57% of its initial output after 10⁵ cycles and resolves four target materials as distinct polarity-amplitude classes at 70 mm. Because the discriminating information lies in the waveform morphology, a generic one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) fed with raw voltage traces classifies the four materials at 90.5% mean accuracy without hand-crafted features. We use this output to drive material-specific robot motions and a polarity-gated three-level warning display. Ionic relaxation thus supplies a design degree of freedom that is orthogonal to permittivity, and it turns an electrostatic proximity signal into a material fingerprint that a small decoder can read.

papers.title: Intervention-Robust VLA: Diverse Demonstrations for Robot Deployment with Safety Filters
papers.authors: Tzu-Yuan Huang, Shao-Hsuan Chang, Dai-Jie Wu, Ralf Römer, Yung-Hui Li, Stefan Sosnowski, Angela P. Schoellig, Kenneth Marino, et al.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.

papers.title: Intelligent Automation and Business Process Optimization Across Enterprise Systems
papers.authors: Mahesh Thummala
papers.abstract: The overarching aim of intelligent automation in enterprises is business process improvement. In business practice, enterprise process optimization with intelligent automation is indicated as complex and challenging. Poor enterprise process quality is frequently attributed to manual intervention in enterprise processes. Decision automation is recognized as one of the most significant investment opportunities by a majority of organizations surveyed. Nevertheless, organizations increasingly encounter situations where traditional automation, including robotic process automation, is difficult or simply insufficient. Intelligent automation creates opportunities to utilize operational data from enterprise processes to automatically enhance business processes, potentially accelerating the improvement of process quality and enterprise value. Without process optimization, intelligent automation can propagate errors and create additional risk into enterprise processes. Therefore, methods for process optimization that support decision automation with intelligent automation across enterprise systems represent a major opportunity for improvement. Such methods encompass many aspects of enterprise process management, such as measurement for improvement, control by monitoring for detection of error, and the integration of process mining and process simulation for sharpening the focus of business process improvement efforts.

papers.title: Inject, Encode, Navigate: Feature-Wise Time Injection for Rectified Flow with Bidirectional Feature Encoding
papers.authors: Xiaogang Wang, Debasish Mishra, Jia Hao Toh, Wangsheng Liu, Yash Shah
papers.abstract: Vision-model-based robotic navigation has gained increasing popularity, yet existing approaches still struggle to deliver effective and efficient navigation performance, \textit{e.g.}, diffusion-based policies that require costly iterative denoising. In this work, we propose three improvements to bridge these gaps. First, we adopt a rectified flow framework to reduce the required inference steps to one while achieving comparable or even superior performance. Second, we leverage a bidirectional Mamba-based visual encoder that employs selective state-space modeling to more effectively capture bidirectional temporal dependencies across observation frames, even with longer input sequences. Most importantly, we find that naïvely combining these two components to balance accuracy with inference speed yields no further performance gains or even produces inferior results. Upon extensive analysis, we realized that the root cause lies in the fact that the Hydra-derived temporal context is shared unchanged across all flow timesteps, and timestep information is introduced only within the velocity network. This weak coupling limits the model's ability to adaptively exploit temporal visual features at different flow states. To address this, we propose a feature-wise timestep conditioning design that explicitly conditions the visual embedding on the flow timestep, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation, thereby restoring a meaningful gradient pathway and enabling coherent interaction between the rectified flow and the temporal encoder. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms both baseline and competitive methods.

papers.title: Hybrid robotic-assisted versus laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy for obesity: a 1-year comparative study of perioperative outcomes, weight loss, and obesity-related comorbidities
papers.authors: Yusujiang Tusuntuoheti, Maimaitiaili Maimaitiming, Qiming Huang, Jiaxin Wen, Jing Wu, Kelimu Abudureyimu, Aikebaier Aili
papers.abstract: Background Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) represents the most commonly performed bariatric surgery worldwide. Robotic-assisted sleeve gastrectomy (RSG) has emerged as an alternative approach to conventional LSG. However, its higher cost and uncertain clinical advantages have limited widespread adoption. At our center, a hybrid RSG technique was adopted. Objective The purpose of this study is to compare perioperative outcomes, hospitalization cost, 1-year weight reduction, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) status, diabetes mellitus and hypertension outcomes between hybrid RSG and LSG in patients with obesity. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 85 patients with obesity who underwent hybrid RSG or LSG between January 2023 and May 2024. Baseline characteristics, operative variables, postoperative complications, hospitalization cost, weight loss indices, GERD status, and diabetes mellitus and hypertension outcomes were evaluated through 1-year follow-up. Results Of the 85 patients included, 22 underwent hybrid RSG and 63 underwent LSG. No statistically significant differences were detected in the baseline characteristics between the two groups. Hybrid RSG was associated with longer operative time than LSG (158.41 ± 25.93 vs. 125.48 ± 28.56 min, P < 0.001) and higher hospitalization cost (62180.78 ± 7237.77 vs. 46693.87 ± 6054.18 CNY, P < 0.001). No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in intraoperative blood loss, postoperative hospital stays, complications, reoperation, and mortality, or weight loss outcomes at 6 or 12 months. At 12 months, GERD remission, de novo GERD, diabetes and hypertension remission also showed no statistically significant differences. Conclusion In this cohort, hybrid RSG and LSG were both safe and effective for the treatment of obesity. However, hybrid RSG was associated with significantly longer operative time and higher hospitalization cost. No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in 1-year weight loss and obesity-related comorbidity outcomes. Further studies incorporating adjusted analyses, longer follow-up, and comprehensive cost-effectiveness evaluation are needed.

papers.title: HumanoidPose: Monocular 3D Pose Estimation for Humanoid Robots
papers.authors: Jinlin Gan, Mingzhe Li, Junsheng Zhang, Zhibo Zhou, Jiahan Geng, Yuhua Luo, Changwang Zhang, Chenglu Wen, et al.
papers.abstract: As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.

papers.title: Humanoid robots for safety-critical electrical switching: A perception-informed runtime constraint filter
papers.authors: Songyang Liu, Yu Hou, Yuqing Hu, Shuai Li
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots can reduce personnel exposure in electrical switching, but safe control is challenging because the tool must reach a target switch next to similar devices, where an imprecise operator command can contact a non-target switch. This study proposes a runtime safety filter that checks each operator command during virtual-reality teleoperation of a humanoid robot. The filter integrates a scene model estimated from the robot head camera and a target-conditioned control barrier function quadratic program that keeps the tool away from the non-target switch while passing safe commands unchanged. papers.title: Heterogeneous multi agent shared control with reinforcement learning based authority arbitration for semi closed loop EEG based shared autonomy
papers.authors: Ao Zhang
papers.abstract: EEG-based shared autonomy integrates neural commands with autonomous assistance to improve control reliability under uncertain brain signals. However, EEG commands may exhibit varying confidence levels and conflict with autonomous actions, making dynamic authority allocation a key challenge. This study proposes a conflict-aware, functionally heterogeneous multi-agent shared-control framework with reinforcement-learning-based authority arbitration for semi-closed-loop EEG-based shared autonomy. Rather than jointly training all agents through reinforcement learning, the framework uses a pretrained EEG intention agent, a fixed autonomous control agent, and a reinforcement-learning-based authority-arbitration agent with distinct information sources and decision roles. The EEG intention agent outputs the estimated user action and its confidence score, while the autonomous control agent generates an environment-aware assistive action. The authority-arbitration agent then learns the control mode and user-authority ratio from EEG confidence, action disagreement, task state, and a shared task reward. A feedback-guided mechanism further adjusts subsequent authority allocation according to completed task-state transitions. The method was evaluated on the Kaya MI-BCI Dataset and Mobile BCI Dataset using recorded EEG data in a semi-closed-loop virtual-navigation environment rather than real-time human–BCI interaction. It achieved TSR/CRR values of 91.7%/88.4% and 87.8%/84.5%, respectively. Compared with EEG-TD3 Multi-agent Copilot, the method improved TSR by 1.1 and 1.3% points and CRR by 1.5 and 1.8% points on the two datasets, respectively. It also exceeded the matched single-agent RL arbitration baseline in both TSR and CRR. Feature-space, feature-importance, failure-case, and ablation analyses further examined the roles of EEG confidence, action disagreement, functional decomposition, and feedback-guided adjustment. The results support the feasibility of adaptive authority arbitration within the evaluated semi-closed-loop protocol and provide preliminary evidence for subsequent online closed-loop validation.

papers.title: HermiteTwin: Bicubic Hermite Shell Digital Twins for Contact-Rich Deformable Manipulation
papers.authors: Kangrui Zhang, Mu Huang, Xing Shen, Tiantian Liu, Bo Ren
papers.abstract: While existing methods for reconstructing deformable object manipulation have made impressive progress, they typically represent a thin object with a single particle set that must serve two purposes at once: modeling bending, and resolving contact with the robot. To bridge this gap, we present HermiteTwin, a framework that reconstructs a physical digital twin of a thin deformable object from multiview video of a robot manipulating it. Our key idea is to represent deformation and contact separately, each at its own resolution. The object is simulated as a bicubic Hermite shell, a coarse grid of $C^1$ elements whose nodal positions and derivatives define a smooth surface with Kirchhoff--Love bending, while the gripper acts through dense samples in material space that are captured, clamped, and released, and whose attachment forces reach the shell through the Hermite basis. This decoupling keeps the physical state compact while contact stays fine-grained. We identify effective material and contact parameters with CMA-ES followed by adjoint-based refinement, and drive a reconstructed Gaussian appearance model with the simulated shell. In experiments on real cloth and foam manipulation, HermiteTwin outperforms the state-of-the-art spring--mass twin across reconstruction, resimulation, and future prediction.

papers.title: Geo-Force: A Theory of Force Sensing from Object Geometry
papers.authors: Abdullah Ayad
papers.abstract: Robots need contact forces to handle delicate objects, but tactile sensors are fragile and hard to integrate, whereas depth sensors, such as RGB-D cameras, are widely available. A virtual touch sensor that keeps the sensing surface of a tactile sensor but replaces its electronics with a touch signal predicted from the target object's geometry, as measured by a depth sensor, could close this gap, yet it is unclear what such a virtual sensor computes and when its output can be trusted. We give a formal answer. We define the Geometric Force as the force on each taxel of a virtual touch sensor, computed in three steps: rendering the surface to be touched as seen from the virtual sensor, predicting the touch signal with a touch map, learned or simulated, and estimating the force from that signal. We prove three properties of the Geometric Force. First, its force vectors only rotate under a change of coordinate frame. Second, it vanishes when the rendered surface does not touch the virtual sensor. Third, it is stable: its error grows at most linearly with the errors of the three steps for Lipschitz maps. The rendering error, in turn, depends on how well the surface is sampled or reconstructed and how accurately the sensor is placed. We then show a fundamental limit: geometry does not reveal the object's stiffness, so no touch map can predict touch exactly for objects of the same shape and different stiffness. Under an elastic contact model, all object-specific knowledge resides in the touch map. From these results, we derive requirements on the depth sensor and the objects, design rules, and the conditions under which such a virtual sensor fails.

papers.title: Generalist Action Critic: Harnessing Frontier Models in Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Yun Yan, Shizhi Hu, Zhichao Li, Yang Guan, Shiqi Liu, Jiaxin Gao, Xiangteng Zhang, Wenbo Ding, et al.
papers.abstract: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.

papers.title: GenPA: Image Generators as Efficient Robot Policies
papers.authors: Zian Deng, Tianyi Zhang, Zilong Zheng, Ziyu Liu, Tao Zhang, Yao Lyu, Shengbo Eben Li
papers.abstract: Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving 1.7-3.4x speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe.

papers.title: From a single demonstration to a general policy for contact-rich manipulation

papers.abstract: We present a four-stage Learning from Demonstration (LfD) pipeline that incrementally constructs a general policy for multi-stage contact-rich manipulation from a single human demonstration.
