papers.title: FoRe: A Force-Guided Framework for Autonomous Grasp Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Shuai Peng, Yongkai Liao, Yuxin Cheng, Haoyuan Wang, Jian Huang
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach-grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and $π_{0.5}$ on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.

papers.title: FlowPAC: Flow-Guided Visual Pruning and Action Caching for Efficient VLA Inference
papers.authors: Jintao Cheng, Yipu Zhang, Haozhe Wang, Lin Jiang, Jiang Xu, Wei Zhang
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.

papers.title: FlexiCAVE: A Dynamically Configurable High-Resolution Display Facility
papers.authors: Zainab Aamir, Saeed Boorboor, Ahamed Shoaib, Arie E. Kaufman
papers.abstract: Large high-resolution displays (LHRDs) are increasingly central to visualization and visual analytics, offering expansive visual space, simultaneous support for context and detail, and intuitive physical navigation. While advances in resolution and form factor have broadened their use, a persistent challenge remains: most LHRDs adopt static geometries, and even reconfigurable systems typically treat layout adjustment as a setup mechanism rather than as an interaction technique during active analysis. To address this, we introduce the FlexiCAVE, a dynamically reconfigurable LHRD environment featuring rotatable display columns that enable real-time adjustment of horizontal curvature. The system comprises forty high-pixel-density panels arranged across ten columns, providing active stereo visualization at approximately 83 million pixels. Each column rotates inward up to 90°, allowing the display to transform between flat and highly curved layouts during active use. It also enhanced users’ sense of direction, with participants reporting that the physical display structure provided directional anchoring absent in static systems. We further explored PIVoT (Physical Interaction to Virtual Transformation), mapping physical display rotation to visualization updates. Our findings reveal that physical reconfiguration is most effective when display geometry provides spatially meaningful correspondence to data operations. We derive design principles for reconfigurable display environments and discuss implications for next-generation large-scale visualization systems.

papers.title: EvoTER: Evolving Embodied Agents via Tool-Use Experience and Reflection
papers.authors: Yingting Zhou, Yuyin Zhou, Yongliang Wang, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao
papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to ground instructions in changing observations, coordinate heterogeneous tools, and recover from failures that can propagate through downstream operations. EvoTER operates through a three-role evolution loop: Explorer records tool-use trajectories; Diagnoser distills successful and failed executions into skills for tool selection, parameter computation, postcondition checks, and recovery; and Validator retains candidate revisions only when they improve complete-task success in fresh sessions. papers.title: EgoSurgHands: An Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Dataset & Benchmark for Open Surgery Training

papers.title: Ego2Ego: Generative Visual Perspective Taking Across Collaborators
papers.authors: Chuhan Jiao, John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Guy Rosman, Andreas Bulling
papers.abstract: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.

papers.title: EfficientDexGrasp: Diverse and Physically Feasible Dexterous Grasping via Few-Step Diffusion Distillation

papers.abstract: Diffusion models dominate dexterous grasp generation, but their iterative sampling is too slow for latency-sensitive deployment. Distilling a multi-step diffusion teacher into a few-step student exposes two coupled failure modes: distinct grasp modes collapse into a single averaged pose that corresponds to no valid grasp, and the physical refinement the teacher performs at every denoising step is lost, so many student predictions drift into penetration or self-collision. We propose EfficientDexGrasp, a physics-guided distillation framework that addresses both. Contrastive energy distillation shapes an auxiliary energy landscape in which distinct grasp modes remain separate low-energy basins. Gated physics-guided consistency trajectory distillation scales correction with how much worse the student is than the teacher, so predictions at or beyond the teacher’s level receive progressively less. The two modules reinforce each other: correction stays on genuinely degraded predictions and leaves the multimodal structure intact. On DexGraspNet, MultiDex, RealDex, and DexGRAB, EfficientDexGrasp achieves 11×to 69× inference speedups and surpasses the strongest prior baselines by 3.8 to 5.8 points on the stringent Suc.6 metric in the 8-step setting. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. papers.title: Driving Intelligence: The Amber Book
papers.authors: Gabriel Seiberth, J. Mark Bishop
papers.abstract: Driving Intelligence examines artificial intelligence through the lens of autonomous driving, using driving as a real-world test case for intelligence. At a time when expectations of artificial general intelligence are rising, the book challenges how intelligence is defined and measured, arguing that current benchmarks saturate, leak, and can be gamed. The book develops a framework for understanding intelligence through the concept of real-world agency, with autonomous driving as its central case study. It argues that driving uniquely combines scale, open-ended environmental complexity, and continuous multi-agent interaction under uncertainty. Unlike most AI benchmarks, which are static or isolated, autonomous driving unfolds in a dynamic physical and social world that cannot be exhaustively specified in advance. The book analyzes failure modes in perception, prediction, planning, and interaction, showing how these limitations reveal a deeper gap between statistical learning from large-scale data and genuine agency. This volume, Amber, benchmarks today's autonomous driving systems against real-world performance data and tracks the shift from language-based AI toward Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems in robotics. The book's central contribution is to reframe autonomous driving as a benchmark for intelligence grounded in real-world agency. It identifies systematic limitations in current AI approaches and clarifies what is missing for genuine autonomy, providing a concrete framework for evaluating progress in Real-World AI and Physical AI. The book will be essential reading for professionals, academics, and students working and researching AI and autonomous vehicles, as well as the interested general reader.

papers.title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
papers.authors: Jiahao Wang, Ming F. Li, Han Xu
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.

papers.title: DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION OF AN INTEGRATED SURVEILLANCE SYSTEM FOR MARITIME ANTI-PIRACY
papers.authors: Sergiu Lupu, Ovidiu Cristea, CLARA-GEORGETA LIȚU, Andrei Pocora, NICOLAE-SILVIU POPA, CLAUDIA LAURENŢA POPESCU
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of piracy remains a critical priority for global maritime security. This article introduces an innovative concept for anti-piracy countermeasures, inspired by conventional methods but automated through an integrated surveillance system. The solution correlates and processes data from navigation devices and multiple sensors, eliminating the need for armed Vessel Protection Detachments or private security guards. The system used to simulate efficiency includes a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, two cameras, proximity sensors, power actuators, and a laser for deterrence. On a real-life scale, the architecture is adaptable to each vessel, optimizing existing on-board hardware resources for autonomous and efficient protection.

papers.title: BronchoVR: An Immersive VR Simulation for Bronchoscopy and Fibreoptic Intubation Training
papers.authors: Muhammad Saad Khan, BRIAN J. ROBINSON, Stuart Marshall, Joaquim Armando Jorge, Craig Anslow
papers.abstract: Fibreoptic intubation (FOI) is an important airway-management skill that requires anaesthetists to navigate a flexible scope through patient-specific anatomy using an indirect, monitor-mediated view. Developing proficiency requires hands-on practice, yet opportunities for clinical training are limited. We present BronchoVR, an immersive VR training prototype developed through consultation with practising specialist anaesthetists and informed by the FOI literature. BronchoVR provides an operating-theatre environment and integrates a patient-specific airway model reconstructed from CT, monitor-mediated scope navigation, and a gamified precision task for practising scope-control skills. These features address requirements for anatomical realism, indirect visual guidance, and psychomotor training. BronchoVR supports rehearsal of FOI navigation and scope handling while preserving the monitor-mediated viewing and hand–eye coordination used during FOI.

papers.title: BeyondEgo: Learning to Act Beyond Egocentric Perception via Humanoid Ego-Exo Foresight
papers.authors: Zhaoshan Yang, Chenglei Li, Haoyu Lei, Yutao Zhang, Yuyu Yang, Zhuo Chen, Ling Ding, Zhongxing Ren, et al.
papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating whole-body motion to perform manipulation tasks in complex environments. Yet egocentric vision-language-action (VLA) policies can miss critical body--scene relationships, and action imitation alone provides no explicit supervision for future scene evolution. We propose BeyondEgo to extend VLA perception in space and time. Spatially, we encode a synchronized exocentric view with frozen DINOv3 and concatenate the resulting tokens with egocentric VLM tokens to condition the action expert. Temporally, we use future observations from both views as privileged supervision for a residual adapter on task-conditioned VLM features. A foresight expert regresses DINOv3 representations of both views 0.6s ahead. At deployment, the foresight expert is discarded and the 4.2M-parameter adapter is retained. We also introduce HELM, to our knowledge, the first closed-loop humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark with synchronized egocentric and exocentric views across five whole-body tasks. On HELM, BeyondEgo improves success from 48.0% to 92.0% in distribution and from 23.5% to 65.0% on 200 held-out scenes with layout, asset, material, and lighting shifts. Ablations show that dual-view DINOv3 foresight yields the best transfer results.

papers.title: Beyond Linear Decodability: Understanding and Improving Instruction Following in World Action Models
papers.authors: Bokai Ji, Jiapeng Chen, Yi Zhang, Zeyuan Ding, Yong Dai, Xiaozhu Ju, Jian Tang, Lemao Liu, et al.
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) exhibit strong manipulation capabilities yet often fail to follow test-time language instructions. Prior work shows that non-following (NF) WAMs encode information about the instructed target, but this information does not control their behavior. By comparing NF WAM with its instruction-following (IF) counterpart, we find that target information is substantially more linearly decodable in IF WAMs, despite being encoded in both. Motivated by this observation, we introduce linear decodability supervision (LDS), a simple yet effective auxiliary training objective that promotes the linear decodability of the instructed target information. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0-$Δ$ with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6% and a grounding rate of 89.2%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. The effectiveness of LDS challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, we propose a prior-instruction competition mechanism, which explains NF and IF behavior as arising from the dominance of prior and instruction signals, respectively. We provide causal evidence for this mechanism by evaluating two training-free interventions derived from it. We reinterpret LDS through this mechanism, showing that it acts as a form of instruction signal enhancement. Finally, more comprehensive evaluations across diverse manipulation tasks and visual domains demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of LDS.

papers.title: Beyond Future Views: Exploring Future-State World Models for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.authors: Kangyi Wu, Pengna Li, Yucheng Wang, Yance Fang, Xihan Ma, Zhizhong Su, Yang Wu, Ye Deng, et al.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.

papers.title: Belief-Driven Quantum Magnetometer Control for GPS-Denied Navigation
papers.authors: Murtuza Lemonwala, Laxima Niure Kandel
papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles increasingly need to navigate without satellite positioning. Magnetic anomaly navigation (Mag-Nav) with quantum magnetometers offers a passive, unjammable fix, but the low size-weight-and-power (SWaP) sensors that small drones can carry are weak, and they are operated open loop at a fixed setting. Interferometric (Ramsey) magnetometers face a trade-off: long interrogation times are more sensitive but become ambiguous when the expected field is uncertain. The navigator's own position belief, pushed through the anomaly map, predicts that field. We close this loop. The filter's predictive field distribution sets the Ramsey phase and interrogation time at every epoch, through a closed-form rule that moves between an ambiguity limit and a decoherence limit. We evaluate it on real U.S. Air Force flight data (real tracks, inertial drift, measured fields, and a survey map tested 18 months after it was flown), with only the Ramsey sensor modelled. Against fixed-setting baselines, 63 of 72 independent flight windows favour belief driven sensing ($p = 2 \times 10^{-11}$). Error falls by 20-27% for low-SNR sensors and 30-44% for mid-contrast sensors. An ablation separates the two ingredients. Phase alignment drives the gain in steady flight, and the rule matches the best fixed setting without the hindsight tuning that setting requires. After a lost start, interrogation time adaptation is essential, cutting median error by 37-42% even against hindsight-tuned phase-aligned settings. Gains are small for high-quality sensors with accurate maps. On an IBM superconducting qubit, the rule's interrogation time stays within $1.3\times$ of the empirical optimum. Coupled with information-aware routing, belief-driven sensing lowers mission error by 15-40%.

papers.title: Bel: Step-Level Policy Improvement of Visual Agents Without Training
papers.authors: Jiajun Fan, Ziwen Wang, Zhaoyu Zhu, Changyi Yang, Neil He, Chaoran Cheng, Ge Liu
papers.abstract: A visual agent acts on what it sees: it taps and types on a screen, or points on a camera image to show a robot where to act. One wrong step can fail its task, yet the right action is often among its own samples, passed over by its greedy decode. Choosing it is a visual judgment, since an action is best judged where it acts, not by its text or coordinates alone: as text, a tap is two numbers; drawn on the screen, it is the Post button of an empty draft. We find that this is decisive: given the screenshot and a tap's coordinates, a decision model chooses among GUI-R1-3B's samples significantly worse on average than when the tap is drawn where it lands. Bel turns this finding into a method that trains nothing and needs only a frozen policy's samples and an image on which each action can be drawn. It marks each candidate on its own copy of the image it acts on, asks a decision model for the probability that executing it is the right decision, so that every kind of action shares one scale, and acts on another candidate only when greedy scores below a threshold and trails it by a margin. On recorded GUI steps, for each of three policies, Bel significantly beats greedy decoding on mobile, web and desktop screens alike and, on the same candidates, gives each a significantly higher mean step success than voting, CATTS, the trained GUI-Critic-R1 and two prompted Qwen3-VL judges shown the same marks; it also significantly improves the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B on every step-level test set. With GUI-R1-3B's thresholds unchanged, Bel significantly raises live AndroidWorld and MiniWoB++ task success for two other policies and robot-pointing success for three policies on each of two groups of benchmarks. Judging each action where it acts thus gives step-level policy improvement of visual agents without training, with significant gains for GUI agents and robot pointing.

papers.title: BRINA: Bottom-Referenced Inertial Navigation with AKAZE, a Sonar SLAM for Autonomous Marine Vehicles
papers.authors: Adolfo Damiano Cafaro, Patrizio Mariani, Roberto Galeazzi
papers.abstract: Forward-looking sonar (FLS) provides reliable underwater perception where optical sensing is limited, but its use for navigation is hindered by the unobserved elevation of each return. As a result, motion estimated directly from sonar images suffers from an unknown metric scale that is commonly resolved using a Doppler velocity log (DVL). We present BRINA (Bottom-Referenced Inertial Navigation with AKAZE), a sonar-inertial SLAM system for marine vehicles that uses the FLS as its only exteroceptive sensor. BRINA estimates the sonar altitude from the first seabed return in each beam and uses it to project matched features onto the seabed, providing metric odometry without a DVL. We further derive a bound relating the remaining scale error to seabed tilt and slope variability. The method is evaluated in simulation with an autonomous underwater vehicle, and in field experiments with uncrewed surface vehicles over ten missions, using two FLS systems under different operating conditions.

papers.title: Autonomous Robots Enabling Smart, Data-Driven Railway Maintenance
papers.authors: Vivien Lacorre, Krister Wolff, Louis-Romain Joly
papers.abstract: Railway transport is essential for sustainable mobility, but increased utilization accelerates infrastructure wear, raising maintenance demands that must be met without compromising availability or cost-efficiency. Emerging technologies in digitalization, AI, and robotics offer promising solutions, yet flexible, on-track inspection systems remain underexplored. This paper presents the development of lightweight, rail bound Multi-Purpose Inspection Robots (MPIRs) designed as research platforms for autonomous data acquisition in railway environments. Two prototypes are currently being developed in Sweden and France within the FP3-IAM4RAIL project. Initial field tests confirm the robots’ ability to autonomously navigate and acquire data at target locations. By combining robotic inspection with AI-based analytics and predictive modeling, this approach aims to enable more flexible, on-demand diagnostics across railway networks, supporting predictive maintenance frameworks.

papers.title: Augmenting Data Physicalization Using Visuo-Tactile Illusions
papers.authors: Xiaojiao Du, Kadek Ananta Satriadi, Adam Drogemuller, James A. Walsh, Ross Smith, Andrew Cunningham
papers.abstract: Data physicalizations fabricated by 3D printers are limited in their ability to dynamically vary their form and tactile properties without refabrication, thereby hindering reusability. In particular, tactile properties on the surface of a physicalization (i.e., surface roughness ) cannot be dynamically adjusted as the data change. To address this limitation, we explore a novel method to increase the reusability of a data physicalization, namely perceived tactile modulation (PTM). Our method enables the perception of varying surface roughness levels on a static data physicalization through the use of virtual reality. By altering the visual roughness of the virtual model, we modulate the user’s perception of tactile roughness, thereby influencing how the physicalization is interpreted through touch and expanding the range of ordinal data values that can be encoded. We conducted two studies to design and evaluate this method. In the first study (N = 20), Just Noticeable Differences (JNDs) were established for perceivable visuo-tactile channels in virtual reality environments. The second study (N = 12) investigates the application of our method across two levels of interactive representation: static and interactive. Our findings show that PTM can reliably modulate perceived roughness in static physicalization, while its effectiveness for supporting dynamic, single-artifact updates (interactive encoding) requires further investigation. We present a series of recommendations for applying PTM techniques in data physicalization.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Child Online Safety: A Dual Perspective on Opportunities and Challenges
papers.authors: Sabira S. Ojagverdiyeva
papers.abstract: Modern children are growing up in a digital world that offers immense potential, with many beginning to use technology from an early age. This digital environment presents countless opportunities for learning and development, but it also necessitates a balanced, thoughtful approach to raising children as informed, open-minded citizens. Industry 4.0, driven by artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT), is reshaping how children think, learn, and interact with the world. The integration of AI into children's lives is a complex issue, bringing both significant benefits and notable risks. On the positive side, AI can power educational tools, interactive games, and personalized learning experiences, fostering cognitive development and creativity. However, it also introduces serious concerns, such as exposure to cyber threats, potential manipulation, privacy violations through data collection, and increased access to harmful content. This study explores the dual impact of information technologies on children's digital development. It examines the primary cybersecurity challenges children face and assesses how AI can both enhance and jeopardize their well-being. By analyzing these multifaceted dynamics, the research aims to offer recommendations for maximizing the advantages of the digital age while ensuring a safer and more supportive online environment for children.

papers.title: AnyBodyCodec: A Shared Native Interface for Body-Model Conversion, Extension, and Humanoid Control
papers.authors: Qianxing Li
papers.abstract: Parametric body models expose incompatible pose and shape controls, tying humanoid policies to particular input formats. AnyBodyCodec learns a shared representation through native conversion, then reuses it for new body models and control with its core frozen. Encoders map MHR, SMPL-X, and SOMA to aligned slots; native decoders recover target controls. The 1.090M-parameter converter covers nine routes and reaches 16.801 mm input-reference MPJPE across six cross routes: the 2.887M Transformer bank reaches 16.390 mm and its parameter-matched version 18.866 mm. Three measured routes take 7.43-7.67 ms on an RTX 4090. Adding ANNY shows that comparable conversion accuracy can accompany different action consistency under one frozen controller. Under a matched PPO budget, aligned slots support 60.78% full-action success across three formats. Separate 160-hour training reaches 66.10% source-weighted validation success, and the controller is deployed qualitatively on a physical G1 through three visual front ends. Together, these results establish reuse through both native geometric fidelity and downstream policy compatibility.

papers.title: Analysis of Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Stefan de Lasa, Mohammadreza Mofayezi, Gennady Pekhimenko, Nandita Vijaykumar
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.

papers.title: An introduction to zero-order optimization techniques for robotics
papers.authors: Armand Jordana, Jianghan Zhang, Joseph Amigo, Ludovic Righetti
papers.abstract: Zero-order optimization techniques are becoming increasingly popular in robotics due to their ability to handle non-differentiable functions and escape local minima. These advantages make them particularly useful for trajectory optimization and policy optimization. In this work, we propose a mathematical tutorial on random search. It offers a simple and unifying perspective for understanding a wide range of algorithms commonly used in robotics. Leveraging this viewpoint, we classify many trajectory optimization methods under a common framework and derive novel competitive RL algorithms.

papers.title: An Autonomous Adaptive Learning System for Robotic Grasping in the Circular Factory
papers.authors: Yitian Shi, Rosa Wolf, Rania Rayyes
papers.abstract: Linear manufacturing typically operates in highly structured settings with standardized objects, allowing robots to execute pre-programmed motions based on precise models. In contrast, circular manufacturing involves dynamic and less controlled environments, where product components can vary due to appearance and physical changes across different product generations. In this context, uncertainty arises from both the unknown or partially observed states of components (e.g., damaged surfaces, altered shapes) and the unstructured disassembly environment, often characterized by heavy clutter, occlusions, and limited sensing viewpoints. This demands a flexible and adaptable robotic grasping system that can cope with unexpected object changes. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an autonomous grasp learning framework designed for highly uncertain and variable conditions. The framework explicitly distinguishes between uncertainty due to noisy or incomplete sensory observations (aleatoric uncertainty) and uncertainty due to limited knowledge and distribution shift (epistemic uncertainty). Moreover, the framework employs an active perception strategy to reduce visual ambiguity: semantic and spatial scene understanding is achieved using vision language models (VLMs), while view planning enables the robot to adjust its viewpoint to improve observability. In addition, the approach leverages large-scale human demonstration data to learn interaction patterns, which are then transferred to robotic end-effectors, enabling robust manipulation in these variable settings. Quantitative validation, including the utility of active vision on disassembled components in practice, is expected to form an important part of future work.

papers.title: Adesktop learning factory for smart and resilient manufacturing based on digital twin and AI
papers.authors: Wenxuan Hu, Zhuoxuan Cao, Achraf El Messaoudi, Peilin Li, Zhiguo Zeng
papers.abstract: Learning factories have been increasingly applied in engineering research and education. In this paper, we develop a small-scale, low-cost, fully open-sourced learning factory that leverages AI and digital twins to demonstrate smart and resilient manufacturing. The learning factory consists of an AGV, three robots, two conveyors and their digital twins. Three typical use cases are designed to demonstrate the capabilities of the learning factory, i.e., material sorting through computer vision-based robot control, coordinating AGV, robots and conveyors for assembly, and digital twin-driven predictive maintenance. The results show that the developed learning factory can adequately support the teaching and research activities on digital twins and AI on manufacturing. Its fully open-source architecture and relatively low deployment cost make it an ideal solution for universities and research institutions.

papers.title: AceVLN: Asynchronous Cloud Edge Deployment of VLNs via Latent Scheduling and Compensation
papers.authors: Zihao Zheng, Hangyu Cao, Yulong Han, Xichang Wu, Zhihao Mao, Maoliang Li, Jiayu Chen, Hailong Zou, et al.
papers.abstract: Cloud--edge deployment enables asynchronous dual-system VLN on resource-constrained robots, but inference and communication delays cause latent mismatch and navigation errors. Existing adaptation methods reuse historical guidance but cannot provide updated navigation information when it becomes inadequate. We propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and edge-side compensation. Our analysis reveals that action-relevant mismatch is concentrated in a compact Critical Subspace and can be tracked through fast-system feature drift. Critical Feature Drift Entropy reflects navigation sensitivity and guides adaptive refresh, while Critical Drift Continuity indicates when recent latent updates can support compensation during latency spikes. AceVLN integrates subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh scheduling, and continuity-guided compensation. Experiments show that \textit{AceVLN} improves success rates by 1.7--2.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines, while reducing amortized computation time by 2.7--10.0\% and FLOPs by 18.4--22.3\%.

papers.title: ADEPT: Adaptive Monocular Depth Estimation via Model-In-The-Loop Photometric Tuning with Capture Risk Prediction
papers.authors: GiHyun Kim, JinMo Yang, Hyung-Sin Kim
papers.abstract: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.

papers.title: A world model for longitudinal health-trajectory prediction in older adults across multinational cohorts
papers.authors: Jingyi Wu, Chenghua Guo, Qianlin Zuo, Pengfei Li, Luxia Zhang
papers.abstract: Aging is characterized by continuously evolving health states, yet most existing prediction models focus on static health risk at isolated time points rather than explicitly modelling how health trajectories unfold over time. We developed a health world model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture to represent evolving health states and simulate future trajectories under specified actions. The model combines a state encoder, an action- and context-conditioned predictor, a stop-gradient target encoder, and clinical outcome heads. We trained the model on the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and evaluated it without refitting in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Open-loop evaluation assessed discrimination and calibration for mortality and worsening of activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). In the held-out HRS test set, the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) for mortality, ADL worsening, and IADL worsening were 0.89, 0.93, and 0.93 at the first horizon and 0.84, 0.84, and 0.85 at the fifth horizon, respectively. Predicted risks stratified subsequent outcomes across horizons. Across the evaluated horizons, mortality AUROC ranged from 0.867 to 0.881 in ELSA and from 0.796 to 0.801 in CHARLS. Simulated trajectories preserved the expected risk ordering across predefined action regimes. In counterfactual simulations, changes in lifestyle actions shifted predicted risks in directions consistent with observed associations. The model provides a framework for longitudinal risk prediction and action-conditioned simulation in older adults.

papers.title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models
papers.authors: Huiyuan Tian, Chih-Yung Wen, Shijian Li
papers.abstract: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.

papers.title: A Hybrid Multi-Goal Path Planning Framework for Powered Wheelchairs in Dynamic Environments: From Simulation to Real-World Validation
papers.authors: Damla Leblebicioğlu, Ege Özgül, Taşkın Padır
papers.abstract: Autonomous powered wheelchairs (PWs) operating in human-centered environments must combine efficient multi-destination path planning with continuous collision avoidance strategies in the presence of static and dynamic obstacles. This study presents a hybrid framework integrating Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP)-based global task ordering, Potential-Field (PF) guidance, and local Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) planners. PF guidance transfers global path information to local planners, helping the robot stay aligned with the global path during obstacle avoidance. Local planning is enhanced with direction-aware, extended-neighborhood A* or RRT using environment-aware sampling and two-step extension. The TSP-PF-RRT and TSP-PF-A* methods are evaluated in normal, crowded, and extra-crowded simulation environments using point-based and elliptical robot models. The elliptical model accounts for platform dimensions during collision avoidance phase. Hardware tests on the physical PW use motion capture (MoCap) for ground-truth measurements, while outside-MoCap experiments rely on onboard LiDAR and RGB-D sensing. Results show that incorporating the wheelchair geometry changes the observed collision behavior, yielding comparable collision avoidance performance between the two hybrid planners under the elliptical model.

papers.title: $γ$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence
papers.authors: Xiaotao Zhang, Lin Qian, Hao Zhang, Xuanrui Cui, Yuehao Huang, Yunzi Wu, Yucheng Deng, Jiankun Dong, et al.
papers.abstract: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $γ$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.
